title: Log Measurements with Python
text:
Progression

Begin with a small teacher-provided dataset such as time, voltage, current, and temperature.
Identify the independent variable, dependent variables, units, expected ranges, and missing-value rule.
Write a Python program that appends one complete row to a CSV file.
Add a timestamp and a clear header row.
Reject values outside the teacher-approved range instead of silently saving them.
Open the CSV in a text editor and spreadsheet to confirm that the structure is portable.
Commit the program and a small non-private sample dataset.

Keep raw data unchanged. If you clean or transform it, save the result as a new file and document what changed.

title: Log Measurements with Python
text:
Evidence
Submit the Python file, sample CSV, terminal output from a successful run, and a data dictionary explaining each column and unit.

title: Log Measurements with Python
text:
Extend your learning

Read Python’s official csv module documentation.
Add command-line arguments for the output filename.
Record a sensor simulation at a fixed interval without connecting physical hardware yet.

title: Log Measurements with Python
text:
Review and reflect
Why are units and column names part of the data? Why should raw measurements be preserved before analysis?

title: Publish Your Quarto Site with GitHub Pages
text:
Publish safely
Before publishing, remove student numbers, private IP addresses, passwords, Wi-Fi information, tokens, and identifiable information about other students. Use a teacher-approved GitHub identity and repository.
Follow this progression:

Render and test the complete site locally.
Run git status and inspect every file that will be committed.
Commit the tested source.
Create or connect the GitHub repository.
Push the source branch.
Publish using the classroom Quarto GitHub Pages method.
Open the public URL in a private browser window and test every page.
Make one small improvement, commit it, push it, and confirm the public site updates.

The class will use one publishing method consistently. Do not switch between a docs folder, a gh-pages branch, and a GitHub Action unless the teacher changes the class workflow.

title: Networking, SSH, and tmux
text:
Progression

Use the GUI to identify the active connection and local IPv4 address.
Confirm the hostname and addresses with hostname, ip address, and ip route.
Use ping only with a teacher-approved host to test reachability.
Connect to the assigned host using ssh user@host.
Immediately run hostname, whoami, and pwd so you know which computer, account, and directory you are controlling.
Create a named tmux session, open a second window, detach, and reattach.
Join a teacher-approved shared session with a partner. Communicate before typing because both users can affect the same terminal.
Exit the remote session cleanly and confirm that you are back on the local computer.

Do not scan the network, attempt unknown accounts, share passwords, expose SSH to the public internet, or use another student’s session without permission.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce
text: Linux Mint is a Linux operating system that usually just works and is easy for new users. We are installing Linux Mint 22.3 “Zena” Xfce Edition. Xfce has a familiar, classic Windows-like layout and uses fewer system resources, which makes it a good fit for our older computers with less than 8 GB of RAM.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce
text:
Class materials

Linux Start Here slides
Linux Mint Installation Reflection


Choose Erase disk and install Linux Mint only on the classroom computer assigned by your teacher. This deletes Windows, accounts, programs, and every file on the selected drive. Stop and ask your teacher before continuing if you are not certain that the computer and drive are approved.







TipLEVEL 4+: MAKE THE INSTRUCTIONS BETTER



If anything here is unclear, incomplete, or could be explained better, improve it in your own copy. Use Suggesting mode if it is available. Otherwise, add a clearly labelled “Suggested improvement” with your revised wording. Include one sentence explaining why your version is clearer or more useful. Do not remove required work. This classroom guide is adapted from the official Linux Mint Installation Guide. The installer screenshots come from that guide. Screens can change slightly between releases, and the example names or checkboxes shown in a screenshot may not match our required classroom settings. Follow the written choices on this page.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce
text:
Before you begin
You need:

the assigned classroom computer;
a Linux Mint 22.3 “Zena” Xfce USB installer signed out from your teacher;
the classroom Wi-Fi credentials; and
your copy of the Linux Mint Installation Reflection.

Disconnect any personal USB drives or external storage. Have the teacher confirm the target computer before you erase anything.

How the classroom USB was made
The teacher, with help from student volunteers, prepared the bootable USB drives before this lab. They downloaded the Linux Mint Xfce .iso image from the official Linux Mint download page and used balenaEtcher to write the image to a USB drive. On Windows, Rufus is another good tool for creating a bootable USB.
An ISO cannot simply be copied onto a USB like an ordinary file. A tool such as Etcher or Rufus writes the image in a form the computer can start from. This process erases the USB drive, so do not try it with a personal drive unless its contents are safely backed up.
For this lab, sign out a prepared USB from your teacher. Record its number if your class uses numbered drives, and return it when the installation is complete.


Working at home: Windows and Mac options
In class, we are installing Linux Mint directly on approved classroom computers. Do not erase or dual boot a family computer for this course.
If you use Windows 11 or a supported Windows 10 computer at home, the recommended option is Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 (WSL 2) with Ubuntu. It gives you a real Linux command line without replacing Windows. Ask the computer owner for permission because installation requires administrator access and may require a restart.

Open PowerShell as Administrator.
Run:

wsl --install

Restart Windows if asked.
Open Ubuntu from the Start menu.
Create a private Linux username and password. The password will not appear while you type it.
Return to PowerShell and verify the installation:

wsl --list --verbose
wsl --status
If WSL is already installed but Ubuntu is missing, run wsl --list --online, then wsl --install -d Ubuntu. Never use wsl --unregister for this course because it permanently deletes that WSL distribution and its files. Follow the official Microsoft WSL installation guide if your screen differs.
On a Mac, use the built-in Terminal for transferable work such as files, Git, Quarto, Python and SSH. macOS is Unix-like, but it is not Linux. Complete Linux-specific hardware, package, permission and administration activities on the classroom Linux computer or an approved remote Linux host. Apple’s Terminal User Guide is a useful reference.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce
text:
1. Start the live system
Insert the Linux Mint USB drive, then start or restart the computer. You need to choose the USB as the startup device before the existing operating system loads.

On the classroom Intel iMacs and Mac minis

Press the power button or restart the Mac.
Immediately hold Option (⌥) or Alt until Startup Manager appears.
Select the USB drive (it may appear as EFI Boot) and press Enter/Return. If the USB does not appear, stop and ask your teacher.

Apple documents the Option/Alt startup shortcut in its Intel Mac startup-key guide.


On a Windows PC
The startup key is different for almost every manufacturer and model. Common keys include Delete, F1, F2, F10, F11, F12, and Escape.

Watch the first manufacturer-logo screen for a message such as Boot Menu, Boot Options, Setup, BIOS, or UEFI.
Press the listed key repeatedly as the computer starts. Try the one-time Boot Menu first and select the USB drive.
If there is no boot menu, enter the BIOS/UEFI settings and, with teacher approval, temporarily move the USB drive ahead of the internal drive in the boot order. Do not change unrelated settings.

If the key is not shown, search for manufacturer model boot menu key or manufacturer model boot from USB. Include the exact manufacturer and model printed on the computer. The official Linux Mint boot guide also lists common keys.
Choose the normal Start Linux Mint option when the Linux Mint startup menu appears. Linux Mint first opens a live session: a temporary desktop running from the USB drive.
The live session may feel slower than the finished installation, and changes made there are not permanent. If the live session asks for a password, leave it blank and press Enter.
Double-click Install Linux Mint on the desktop.

Select English, then select Continue.



Linux Mint installer language screen with English selected.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce

3. Connect to the classroom Wi-Fi
Select the classroom network and connect using the Wi-Fi credentials given in class.






WarningDo not use guest Wi-Fi



Do not use the guest Wi-Fi. Use only the classroom Wi-Fi credentials provided by your teacher.





Linux Mint installer wireless-network selection screen.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce

4. Install multimedia codecs
Check Install multimedia codecs, then select Continue. Codecs help the computer play common audio and video formats.



Linux Mint installer option to install multimedia codecs.

title: Install Linux Mint 22.3 Xfce
text:
5. Choose the installation type
Select Erase disk and install Linux Mint.

Leave Advanced features at its default setting with None selected. We can explore advanced storage settings in a later lab.
Do not select an encryption option for this classroom installation.
Do not select Something else.
Do not select an “install alongside” option in this lab.




Linux Mint installation-type screen with Erase disk and install Linux Mint selected.


Select Install Now or Continue, depending on the wording shown. Read the drive-change summary, confirm that it refers to the approved classroom drive, and then continue.
In a future lab, we will install another operating system alongside Windows and create a dual-boot computer. That is not today’s task.






WarningDual-boot installations use different instructions



If you are installing Linux on your own computer and want to keep Windows, stop here and do not choose “Erase disk and install Linux Mint.” A dual-boot installation requires a current backup, enough free storage, and a careful plan for the computer’s partitions, encryption, firmware, and recovery options.
It is usually easier to install Windows first and Linux second. Windows installation can replace the existing boot sequence, while Linux Mint normally detects Windows and creates a menu for choosing an operating system at startup. See Linux Mint’s official multi-boot guidance.
Before changing partitions, check whether Windows uses BitLocker/device encryption, save its recovery key, and research the exact computer model. An encrypted Windows drive may prevent a Linux installer from safely examining or resizing the Windows partitions. Ubuntu’s BitLocker dual-boot explanation describes this issue clearly.
Some computers have two internal SSDs. Installing each operating system on a separate drive can make the layout easier to understand and can reduce the chance of accidentally changing the other system’s partitions or boot files. However, this is not a rule of EFI/UEFI, and it is not required on every computer. Firmware behaviour varies, even between Lenovo Legion models, so search the manufacturer, exact model, and terms such as dual boot, UEFI, and boot order before proceeding. Use a model-specific guide and ask for experienced help rather than guessing.

title: Git: Save the History of Your Work
text:
Your first repository
Create a teacher-approved project folder inside your home directory. Configure Git with the classroom identity supplied by your teacher. Do not publish a personal email address.
mkdir -p ~/linux-labs/my-site
cd ~/linux-labs/my-site
git init
printf "# My Technology Site\n" > README.md
git status
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add project README"
git log --oneline
Repeat the cycle after making one small change: edit, git status, review, stage, review the staged change, commit, and inspect the history.

text:
Assignment 1: Make Linux Mint Xfce Your Own






TipLEVEL 4+: MAKE THE INSTRUCTIONS BETTER



If anything here is unclear, incomplete, or could be explained better, improve it in your own copy. Use Suggesting mode if it is available. Otherwise, add a clearly labelled “Suggested improvement” with your revised wording. Include one sentence explaining why your version is clearer or more useful. Do not remove required work. Mr. A will review your change and may update the course website and future assignment documents if he agrees it helps. Improving a real instruction accurately is one way to demonstrate Level 4+ thinking.



Part 2: make Linux feel like your computer






ImportantOpen the assignment and know what to submit



Make a copy of Make Linux Mint Xfce Your Own.
Submit ONE completed Google Doc in Google Classroom. It must contain a BEFORE screenshot, an AFTER screenshot, and all five short reflection answers. Do not attach the screenshots as separate files.




1. Save your BEFORE screenshot
Do this before changing any settings. Sign in to your own Linux account and show the full desktop with its wallpaper and bottom panel visible. Press Print Screen (PrtSc). If nothing happens, try Fn + PrtSc or search the application menu for Screenshot. Save the picture in your Pictures folder and insert it into the assignment Google Doc.






NoteWhat a clear BEFORE screenshot looks like






A typical Linux Mint Xfce desktop before customization, with the wallpaper and full panel visible.


Show the whole desktop, not a cropped corner. Keep the wallpaper and full panel visible. This reference image is not a student submission. Image source: Linuxiac.




2. Get inspiration from Xfce makeovers
Watch the parts that interest you. Use the built-in settings in the next section. You do not need to copy either design, download a theme, run terminal commands, or install Compiz.



Customize Your Linux Mint XFCE: A Simple Guide by Specter-3924 shows a complete Linux Mint Xfce desktop makeover.



Making XFCE Look Better by NH Soft: start at 3:33 for wallpaper, 7:32 for themes, and 12:49 for the panel. Skip downloads, terminal commands, and the later Compiz effects.



Three realistic built-in-only design ideas
Pick one direction or mix ideas. Theme names can vary slightly between classroom computers.









Design direction
Wallpaper
Theme or icons
Panel




Calm study desktop
Choose a quiet nature or abstract built-in image
Try a light Mint-Y style and a simple built-in icon set
Keep it at the bottom and set a comfortable row size around 38 to 42 pixels


Dark coding desktop
Choose a darker built-in image with little visual clutter
Try a built-in dark Mint-Y style and readable icons
Move it to the top or keep it at the bottom, then make it slightly taller


Easy-to-see desktop
Choose an uncluttered image that does not hide labels
Choose the clearest high-contrast built-in style available
Increase the row size to about 46 to 52 pixels and keep the menu, network, sound, and clock easy to find






Example of a clean customized Xfce desktop with a calm wallpaper, tidy File Manager, readable Terminal, and a simple bottom panel.


This course example shows one possible finished direction. Your design should reflect your own choices and remain readable.



3. Make the three required changes
Use the settings already included with Linux Mint. Do not download themes, scripts, packages, or desktop effects without teacher permission.

Change A: wallpaper



Xfce Desktop Settings open to the Background controls and wallpaper choices.



Right-click an empty part of the desktop.
Select Desktop Settings, then Background.
Choose a different built-in picture. Close the window to see the result.

Example: choose a simple image whose light and dark areas still let you read desktop icon labels. Screenshot source: It’s FOSS.


Change B: theme or icons



Xfce Appearance settings open to the Style tab with several built-in themes.



Open Menu > Settings > Appearance. If you cannot find it, type Appearance into the menu search box.
Open the Style tab and try a different built-in style. This changes application windows, menus, buttons, and colours.
You may also open the Icons tab and choose a different built-in icon set. Keep labels and controls readable.

Example: compare one light and one dark Mint-Y variant, then keep the one that gives better contrast with your wallpaper. Screenshot source: Xfce Project.


Change C: panel



Xfce Panel Preferences showing the Display tab and Row size control.



Right-click the bottom panel, which is the bar with the menu and clock.
Choose Panel > Panel Preferences. You can also search for Panel in the menu.
Change the Row size first. A small change, such as 36 pixels to 42 pixels, is easy to see and easy to reverse.
If you want another change, move the panel to the top or adjust its appearance. Close Panel Preferences when finished.

Do not delete the panel or remove the application menu, network, sound, or clock controls. Screenshot source: It’s FOSS.
If a setting looks wrong, return to the same settings window and change it back. If you cannot restore the panel or essential controls, stop and ask for help.



4. Save your AFTER screenshot
Make sure the updated wallpaper and panel are visible. You may leave File Manager open so the theme is also visible. Take another screenshot and insert it into the same Google Doc.


5. Answer all five reflection questions
In your assignment Google Doc, answer:

What wallpaper did you choose, and where did you change it?
What theme or icon change did you make, and which setting did you use?
What did you change about the panel, and how did you do it?
Which change made the desktop look better or easier to use, and why?
Did anything go wrong, and how did you fix it? Write “Nothing went wrong” if appropriate.







NoteOptional customization



After completing the required work, you may change fonts or pointer size, add a favourite application shortcut, arrange desktop icons, or investigate another built-in appearance setting. Do not install a theme or desktop effect without permission.

Otherwise, add a clearly labelled “Suggested improvement” with your revised wording. Include one sentence explaining why your version is clearer or more useful. Do not remove required work. Mr. A will review your change and may update the course website and future assignment documents if he agrees it helps. Improving a real instruction accurately is one way to demonstrate Level 4+ thinking.



Part 5: meet the terminal






ImportantOpen the assignment and know what to submit



Make a copy of Terminal Quest: WSL and Mac Basics.
Submit ONE completed Google Doc in Google Classroom. Paste the complete, reviewed command history into that document. Do not submit a separate history text file.




1. Open the correct terminal

Windows with WSL
Open Start and search for WSL, Ubuntu, or the name of the installed Linux distribution. Open the matching app. Run the Linux assignment commands there, not in PowerShell.
If WSL is not installed, ask the computer owner or teacher for permission. Installation requires administrator access and may require a restart. With permission, open PowerShell as Administrator and run:
INPUT
wsl --install
Restart if Windows asks. If installation is blocked, a security warning appears, or you are unsure which distribution opened, stop and ask for help. Follow the official Microsoft WSL installation guide when needed.


Linux Mint or Ubuntu
Press Ctrl + Alt + T, or search the application menu for Terminal. WSL is not needed on a Linux computer.


Mac
Press Command + Space, search for Terminal, and press Return. You can also open Applications > Utilities > Terminal.



2. Identify the account and current folder
Run one command at a time. Read the result and enter the requested answer in your Google Doc.
INPUT
whoami
INPUT
hostname
INPUT
pwd
INPUT
ls
INPUT
ls -a
EXAMPLE OUTPUT
Desktop  Documents  Downloads  Music  Pictures
Your username, computer name, path, files, and hidden items will differ. A shell prompt may end with $ or %; do not type that prompt symbol as part of a command.


3. Investigate the operating system
INPUT
uname -s
INPUT
uname -m
INPUT
df -h .
INPUT
uptime
Record the system name, machine or CPU type, available space, and uptime in your Google Doc. On a Mac, the system name may be Darwin. In WSL, the system name is normally Linux because Linux is running inside Windows.


4. Create the terminal-quest folder and hello.txt
Run each command separately:
INPUT
cd ~
INPUT
mkdir -p terminal-quest
INPUT
cd terminal-quest
INPUT
pwd
INPUT
echo Hello from my computer > hello.txt
INPUT
ls
INPUT
cat hello.txt
EXAMPLE OUTPUT
Hello from my computer
Return to your home folder and confirm your location:
INPUT
cd ~
INPUT
pwd


5. View running processes
On WSL, Linux Mint, or Ubuntu, try:
INPUT
htop
If htop is not installed, use top, or ask permission before installing software. On Ubuntu-based systems, the approved installation commands are:
INPUT
sudo apt update
INPUT
sudo apt install htop -y
On a Mac, use htop only if it is already installed. Otherwise run:
INPUT
top
Press q to leave htop or top. Observe one CPU and one memory detail. Never end an unfamiliar process. If installation is blocked or asks for access you do not have, use top and ask for help.


6. Review and copy the complete command history
History contains commands, not their output. Review it before copying. Remove or redact passwords, tokens, personal names, private paths, Wi-Fi credentials, and other private information. If you see a password or token, do not paste it. Stop and ask for help, and change any exposed credential.

Windows WSL, Linux Mint, or Ubuntu using Bash
Review the history:
INPUT
history
On Windows WSL, copy the complete history to the Windows clipboard:
INPUT
history | clip.exe
On Linux Mint or Ubuntu, first check the desktop session:
INPUT
echo $XDG_SESSION_TYPE
If the result is x11, ask permission to install xclip if needed, then copy:
INPUT
sudo apt install xclip -y
INPUT
history | xclip -selection clipboard
If the result is wayland, ask permission to install wl-clipboard if needed, then copy:
INPUT
sudo apt install wl-clipboard -y
INPUT
history | wl-copy


Mac using the default zsh shell
Review the complete history:
INPUT
history 1
Copy it to the Mac clipboard:
INPUT
history 1 | pbcopy
If the Mac uses Bash instead of zsh, use history and history | pbcopy.
Paste the complete, reviewed history into the labelled box in your Terminal Quest Google Doc. Confirm that it includes the activities you tried. Review the pasted text again before submitting. Submit only that completed Google Doc.

Bashcrawl is a terminal adventure. Folders are rooms and files contain clues. There is no required final room and no time limit. Explore for as long as you can, return another day if you want, and record the furthest room you reached.


1. Open Terminal and check Git

Windows: Open WSL, Ubuntu, or the installed Linux distribution from Start.
Linux Mint or Ubuntu: Press Ctrl + Alt + T, or open Terminal from the application menu.
Mac: Press Command + Space, search for Terminal, and press Return.

INPUT
git --version
EXAMPLE OUTPUT
git version 2.43.0
Your version may differ. If Git is missing on WSL, Ubuntu, or Linux Mint, ask permission before running sudo apt update and sudo apt install git -y. On a Mac, follow the Apple Command Line Tools prompt only with the computer owner’s permission. Stop and ask for help if installation is blocked.


2. Download and start Bashcrawl
Run one command at a time:
INPUT
cd ~
INPUT
mkdir -p Games
INPUT
cd Games
INPUT
git clone https://gitlab.com/slackermedia/bashcrawl.git
If Bashcrawl is already downloaded in ~/Games, skip the clone command.
INPUT
cd bashcrawl/entrance
INPUT
cat scroll
git clone downloads a working copy of the repository into a new folder. It does not need administrator access. Never add sudo to that command.


3. Explore the dungeon
Useful commands include:
INPUT
pwd
INPUT
ls
INPUT
ls -a
INPUT
cat filename
INPUT
cd directory
INPUT
cd ..
Replace filename and directory with names you actually see. Read every scroll file you find. If a command does not work, read the message, try ls or ls -a, reread the clue, or go back one room. Do not use sudo inside the game.


4. Record and submit your progress
In the Bashcrawl Google Doc:

Record the furthest room or path you reached. Run pwd in that room if you need the path.
Answer what clue, object, or surprise you discovered.
Name one command you learned or used and explain what it does.
Explain what you tried when you got stuck and whether it worked.
Insert at least one readable screenshot showing the terminal at your furthest room or an interesting clue.

title: Ethernet Cable Categories and Speeds
text:
The category printed on the cable describes tested cabling performance. The slowest port, cable path, or device sets the link speed.





Numbered contacts on an 8P8C modular plug.



8P8C, often called RJ45
Eight positions and eight contacts. Keep the pairs twisted close to the plug. Do not judge cable category by colour.
Figure 1. Open source and licence.






Close view of a twisted-pair Ethernet cable and modular plug.



Read the jacket
Look for the category, conductor type, and certification printed along the cable jacket.
Figure 2. Open source and licence.





Cat5e1 Gbps to 100 m. 2.5 or 5 Gbps may work when the equipment and cable meet the standard.


Cat61 Gbps to 100 m. 10 Gbps on shorter runs, commonly up to 55 m in suitable conditions.


Cat6A10 Gbps to 100 m. Thicker and often less flexible.


Cat825 or 40 Gbps to 30 m. Mainly data centres, not a normal classroom patch cable.








NoteWhat about Cat7?



Cat7 appears in retail listings, but it is not the normal ANSI/TIA category choice for a standard RJ45 classroom cable. Prefer a correctly made Cat6 or Cat6A cable for a known requirement.


Class choice: use the cable and plug specified by the teacher. Match the plug to solid or stranded conductors and to the cable diameter.

text:
Power off. Unplug. Control static. Then look inside.
Figure 1. The whole system first. Open image source and licence.
crumbs: 1. Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts

title: Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts
text:
What is inside?


Motherboard
The main circuit board. It connects the CPU, RAM, storage, power, ports, and expansion cards.


CPU
Runs program instructions. A heat sink and fan usually cover it.


RAM
Fast working memory for programs in use now. It clears when power is removed.


Power supply
Converts wall AC to the low-voltage DC used by the computer. Inspect only the outside, cables, and label.


Cooling
Fans, heat sinks, vents, and thermal material move heat away from chips.


Expansion parts
Graphics, Wi-Fi, network, and sound cards add functions. Not every computer has every part.
crumbs: 1. Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts

title: Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts
text:
SSD or spinning hard disk?





A hard disk drive beside a solid-state drive.



HDD: spinning disk
Magnetic platters spin under a moving read/write head. Usually cheaper per terabyte, but slower, noisier, and easier to damage while spinning.
Figure 2. HDD and SSD. Open source and licence.






M.2 solid-state drive circuit board.



SSD: flash storage
Stores data in electronic flash memory. No moving parts. Usually faster, silent, lower-power, and more resistant to bumps.
Figure 3. M.2 SSD. Open source and licence.
crumbs: 1. Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts

title: Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts
text:
How storage connects





The data and power connectors on a SATA solid-state drive.



SATA drive: two connections
SATA data is the narrow 7-pin path to the motherboard. SATA power is the wider 15-pin path to the power supply.
Figure 4. SATA connectors. Open source and licence.






M.2 storage board ready to mount in a motherboard slot.



M.2 drive: mounts on the board
M.2 describes the shape. The drive may use SATA or NVMe/PCIe. The drive and motherboard slot must support the same type.

title: Series-Parallel Circuits
text:
You will identify series and parallel groups, reduce a mixed circuit one group at a time, calculate the total values, and then work back to each resistor. This is useful when one protected power source feeds several loads in a robot, vehicle, computer, or sensor system.
Used in college or university: circuit laboratories, electronics, robotics, instrumentation, and preparation for Kirchhoff’s laws. The same circuit pattern lets cars and robots power several loads from one protected source.
Where you see it: A car uses a fuse and switch to feed parallel lamps or control modules. A robot uses one protected supply for sensors, indicators, and control boards.

title: Series-Parallel Circuits
text:
Start with a real system
A robot may have a fuse, switch, and current-limiting resistor in series with several parallel loads. A vehicle uses the same pattern when one protected supply feeds lamps, sensors, or control modules. The series parts affect every load; each parallel branch still receives the same branch voltage.
For an engaging introduction, watch ElectroBOOM101-005, then use The Organic Chemistry Tutor’s series and parallel explanation or Khan Academy’s circuit review for the calculation steps.

title: Series-Parallel Circuits
text:
Identify the connections
Components are in series when the same current must pass through them. Components are in parallel when both ends connect to the same two nodes. Trace nodes and current paths; do not decide from visual appearance alone.



Figure 1. Series has one current path; parallel has branches connected to the same two nodes. #

title: Series-Parallel Circuits
text:
Rules and equations
For a series group, current is common, voltage drops add, and resistance adds:
\[
I_T=I_1=I_2=\cdots
\tag{1}\]
\[
V_T=\sum_{k=1}^{n}V_k
\tag{2}\]
\[
R_{\mathrm{series}}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}R_k
\tag{3}\]
For a parallel group, voltage is common, branch currents add, and reciprocal resistance adds:
\[
V_T=V_1=V_2=\cdots
\tag{4}\]
\[
I_T=\sum_{k=1}^{n}I_k
\tag{5}\]
\[
\frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{parallel}}}
=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{R_k}
\tag{6}\]
For exactly two parallel resistors:
\[
R_{\mathrm{parallel}}=\frac{R_aR_b}{R_a+R_b}
\tag{7}\]
For any resistor, use Ohm’s law and power:
\[
V_k=I_kR_k
\tag{8}\]
\[
P_k=V_kI_k=I_k^2R_k=\frac{V_k^2}{R_k}
\tag{9}\]

title: Series-Parallel Circuits
text:
Reduce, solve, expand, and check

Mark one true series or parallel group.
Replace it with an equivalent resistance and redraw the whole circuit.
Repeat until only total resistance remains.
Solve the equivalent circuit with \(I_T=V_T/R_T\).
Work backward. Use common current for series parts and common voltage for parallel branches.
Check that branch currents add, voltage drops add around a path, and component powers add to total power.




Figure 2. The common mixed-network pattern used in Questions 1, 2, and 4. #

title: Series-Parallel Circuits
text:
Guided example
A \(10.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source supplies \(R_1=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series with \(R_2=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_3=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in parallel.
Given
\[
V_T=10.0\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
R_1=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega},\qquad
R_2=R_3=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
\tag{10}\]
Unknowns
\[
R_{23},\ R_T,\ I_T,\ V_1,\ V_{23},\ I_2,\ I_3,\ P_T
\tag{11}\]
General equations
\[
R_{23}=\frac{R_2R_3}{R_2+R_3},\qquad
R_T=R_1+R_{23},\qquad
I_T=\frac{V_T}{R_T}
\tag{12}\]
\[
V_1=I_TR_1,\qquad
V_{23}=V_T-V_1,\qquad
I_2=\frac{V_{23}}{R_2},\qquad
I_3=\frac{V_{23}}{R_3}
\tag{13}\]
Substitute and solve
\[
R_{23}=\frac{(2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega})(2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega})}
{2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}+2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}
=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
\tag{14}\]
\[
R_T=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}+1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
\tag{15}\]
\[
I_T=\frac{10.0\,\mathrm{V}}{2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}
=5.0\,\mathrm{mA}
\tag{16}\]
\[
V_1=(5.0\,\mathrm{mA})(1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega})=5.0\,\mathrm{V}
\tag{17}\]
\[
V_{23}=10.0\,\mathrm{V}-5.0\,\mathrm{V}=5.0\,\mathrm{V}
\tag{18}\]
\[
I_2=I_3=\frac{5.0\,\mathrm{V}}{2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}
=2.5\,\mathrm{mA}
\tag{19}\]
\[
P_T=V_TI_T=(10.0\,\mathrm{V})(5.0\,\mathrm{mA})
=50\,\mathrm{mW}
\tag{20}\]
Calculator entries
(2 EXP 3 × 2 EXP 3) ÷ (2 EXP 3 + 2 EXP 3)
10 ÷ (2 EXP 3)
5 ÷ (2 EXP 3)
Check: \(I_2+I_3=5.0\,\mathrm{mA}=I_T\) and \(V_1+V_{23}=10.0\,\mathrm{V}=V_T\).

title: Series-Parallel Circuits
text:
Student questions
Use the student handout for the fillable GUESS tables and work space.

Question 1: reduce one parallel group
A \(12.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source supplies \(R_1=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series with \(R_2=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_3=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance, total current, all resistor voltages and currents, and total power.


Question 2: unequal parallel branches
An \(18.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source supplies \(R_1=3.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series with \(R_2=6.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_3=3.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in parallel. Find \(R_{23}\), \(R_T\), \(I_T\), \(V_1\), \(V_{23}\), \(I_2\), \(I_3\), and \(P_T\). Check current and voltage.


Question 3: two series branches in parallel
A \(24.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source is connected across two branches. Branch A has \(R_1=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_2=3.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series. Branch B has \(R_3=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_4=4.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series. Find the branch resistances and currents, every resistor voltage, total current, equivalent resistance, and total power.



Figure 3. Question 3 has two series branches connected in parallel. #




Question 4: find an unknown branch resistor
A \(20.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source supplies \(R_1=1.2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series with a parallel group. One branch is \(R_2=2.4\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and the other is an unknown \(R_3\). The source current is \(10.0\,\mathrm{mA}\). Find \(V_1\), \(V_{23}\), \(I_2\), \(I_3\), \(R_3\), and \(R_T\).


Question 5: current-limit design
A \(12.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source supplies \(R_S\), \(R_1=330\,\mathrm{\Omega}\), and a parallel load made from \(R_2=680\,\mathrm{\Omega}\) and \(R_3=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\). Find the minimum \(R_S\) that keeps source current at or below \(15.0\,\mathrm{mA}\). Select the next safe standard 5% value, then calculate current, load voltage, branch currents, resistor powers, and suitable power ratings.



Figure 4. Question 5 turns the analysis process into a current-limit design. #

text:
Common voltage
Components are in parallel when both ends connect to the same two nodes. Every branch has the same voltage:



Figure 1. Parallel-circuit reference schematic. Every branch connects to the same two nodes. #


\[
V_k = V_T
\tag{1}\]
crumbs: 1. Package 1: Basic Electricity and Parallel Circuits

title: Parallel Circuits
text:
General parallel rules
The source current is the sum of the branch currents:
\[
I_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} I_k
\tag{2}\]
The equivalent resistance is
\[
\frac{1}{R_T} = \sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{R_k}
\tag{3}\]
For exactly two parallel resistors, the product-over-sum shortcut is
\[
R_T = \frac{R_aR_b}{R_a+R_b}
\tag{4}\]
Calculate any branch current with Ohm’s law:
\[
I_k = \frac{V_T}{R_k}
\tag{5}\]
Total power equals the sum of the branch powers:
\[
P_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n}P_k = V_T I_T
\tag{6}\]

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
You will apply Kirchhoff’s current law at a node and Kirchhoff’s voltage law around a loop. These laws let you write equations for a circuit that cannot be reduced by inspection.
Used in college or university: Nodal analysis, mesh analysis, electronics, power systems, and control hardware. [1, Ch. 9]
Where you see it: In a car wiring harness, current splits between lights and control modules. In a robot, it splits between the controller, sensors, and motors.

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
Kirchhoff’s current law



Figure 1. At a square junction node, total current entering equals total current leaving. #


\[
\sum I_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum I_{\mathrm{out}}
\tag{1}\]
A negative answer means the real current is opposite the arrow you selected.

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
Kirchhoff’s voltage law



Figure 2. Two loops share one resistor and create two simultaneous equations. #


\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\Delta V_k = 0
\tag{2}\]
Choose one loop direction and keep the signs consistent. A source rise is positive; a resistor drop in the current direction is negative.

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
Workflow

Mark the essential nodes and independent loops.
Choose and label unknown current directions.
Write current-law and voltage-law equations.
Replace resistor voltage with \(V=IR\).
Solve without rounding, then check every original node and loop equation.
Build the same network in Tinkercad and compare the simulated values.

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
Worked solutions






NoteQuestion 2: Missing loop voltage





Kirchhoff’s voltage law requires the source rise to equal the voltage drops:
\[
V_3=12.0\,\mathrm{V}-2.4\,\mathrm{V}-4.1\,\mathrm{V}=5.5\,\mathrm{V}.
\tag{3}\]
Check: \(12.0-2.4-4.1-5.5=0.0\,\mathrm{V}\).









NoteQuestion 4: Two loops with two sources





The two loop equations are
\[
5I_1-2I_2=10
\tag{4}\]
\[
-2I_1+7I_2=6.
\tag{5}\]
Solving them gives \(I_1=2.645161\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}\) and \(I_2=1.612903\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}\).
The shared-branch current is
\[
I_3=I_1-I_2=1.032258\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}.
\tag{6}\]
Final answers: \(I_1=2.65\,\mathrm{mA}\), \(I_2=1.61\,\mathrm{mA}\), and \(I_3=1.03\,\mathrm{mA}\).

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
0. Orientation, Safety, and Design







What students learn
Why it matters




Work safely, follow a design process, and document decisions and sources.
Safe, documented work is the foundation for every build, investigation, and engineering decision.



Subsections: Safety; design process; documentation; privacy and attribution
Coming out of this section, students can: Work safely, document decisions, cite sources, and keep a usable design record.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
1. Numbers, Units, and Calculator Skills







What students learn
Why it matters




Use number systems, units, engineering notation, estimates, and a scientific calculator.
Units, scale, estimation, and calculator fluency make technical results understandable and trustworthy.



Subsections: Number systems; units; significant figures; engineering notation; calculator workflow
Coming out of this section, students can: Convert technical quantities, use engineering notation, estimate results, and present calculations clearly.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
2. Electrical Fundamentals







What students learn
Why it matters




Explain and calculate charge, voltage, current, resistance, sources, and loads.
These quantities explain how sources, conductors, and loads behave in a complete circuit.



Subsections: Charge; voltage; current; resistance; sources and loads; AC and DC
Coming out of this section, students can: Explain and calculate charge, voltage, current, resistance, opens, shorts, and source behaviour.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
3. DC Circuit Analysis







What students learn
Why it matters




Analyze direct-current networks, solve their equations, and connect electrical energy to useful work.
Circuit analysis predicts electrical behaviour; an energy-conversion lab shows what that behaviour accomplishes in a real device.



Subsections: Ohm's law; series circuits; parallel circuits; mixed networks; Kirchhoff's laws; linear systems; work, energy, power, and efficiency; dividers; troubleshooting
Coming out of this section, students can: Solve and verify series, parallel, and mixed networks, use linear equations, and compare electrical energy with mechanical work.
Collaboration: The Engineering Preparation Track collaboration map connects this work with TEJ3M/TEJ4M, SPH3U physics, SCH4U chemistry, and SBI4U biology.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
4. Building, Schematics, and Measurement







What students learn
Why it matters




Build readable circuits and compare calculated, simulated, and measured results.
Readable schematics, careful construction, and correct measurement make troubleshooting possible.



Subsections: Breadboards; schematics; simulation; multimeter use; measurement uncertainty
Coming out of this section, students can: Build from a schematic, measure safely, compare predicted and measured values, and locate wiring errors.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
5. Components and Applied Circuits







What students learn
Why it matters




Select and apply common components in useful low-voltage circuits.
Component knowledge lets students select, connect, protect, and test useful electronic circuits.



Subsections: Sensors; batteries; capacitors; diodes; transistors; timers; motors and relays
Coming out of this section, students can: Design and test sensor, timing, switching, power-supply, and actuator-interface circuits.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
6. Digital Logic and Inputs







What students learn
Why it matters




Create stable digital inputs and analyze combinational and sequential logic.
Stable inputs and Boolean logic connect physical switches and sensors to dependable digital decisions.



Subsections: Logic levels; pull-ups and pull-downs; debouncing; logic gates; truth tables; state
Coming out of this section, students can: Build stable switch inputs, complete truth tables, analyze logic, and create a small digital system.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
7. Fabrication and PCBs







What students learn
Why it matters




Turn a tested prototype into a durable fabricated or manufactured result.
Fabrication turns a tested design into a durable, repeatable physical product.



Subsections: Soldering; connectors; PCB design; manufacturing files; enclosures and fabrication
Coming out of this section, students can: Prepare a manufacturable design and produce a soldered, printed, laser-cut, or machined result.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
8. Computer Systems







What students learn
Why it matters




Assemble, commission, maintain, upgrade, and troubleshoot computer hardware.
Computer hardware work connects electrical principles to real systems, maintenance, repair, and reuse.



Subsections: Components; power; assembly; startup; Linux installation; upgrades and troubleshooting
Coming out of this section, students can: Identify, assemble, commission, benchmark, troubleshoot, upgrade, and document a computer.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
section: 9. Linux, Operating Systems and Basic Networking
text:
9. Linux, Operating Systems and Basic Networking







What students learn
Why it matters




Use and administer a Linux system safely from the desktop and command line.
Operating-system knowledge gives students control over files, software, permissions, and system behaviour.



Subsections: Desktop use; files and permissions; command line; software; basic networking; services; backup and recovery
Coming out of this section, students can: Install and use Linux, manage files and permissions, run commands, check basic network settings and connectivity, and complete basic administration.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
10. Programming







What students learn
Why it matters




Write, test, debug, and document programs for calculations, data, and control.
Programming turns a process or calculation into a repeatable tool that can handle inputs and errors.



Subsections: Algorithms; variables; conditions; loops; functions; files; testing and debugging
Coming out of this section, students can: Write, test, debug, and document programs that calculate, model, process data, or control a task.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
11. Microcontrollers







What students learn
Why it matters




Connect code to protected sensors, inputs, outputs, communication, and actuators.
Physical computing joins code, sensors, outputs, timing, and electrical protection in one system.



Subsections: Inputs and outputs; sensors; timing; communication; actuators; state machines; data logging
Coming out of this section, students can: Create a protected sensor-and-actuator system using a microcontroller or single-board computer.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
12. Networking and Administration







What students learn
Why it matters




Explain networks and operate small classroom services using defensive practices.
Networking explains how devices communicate and how small services are operated safely.



Subsections: Addresses; protocols; diagnostics; secure remote access; services; users and backups
Coming out of this section, students can: Configure and diagnose a small network or classroom service using defensive administration practices.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
13. Data Science and Machine Learning







What students learn
Why it matters




Prepare, visualize, model, and evaluate non-personal data responsibly.
Data science helps students turn measurements into evidence while recognizing uncertainty and bias.



Subsections: Data preparation; visualization; regression; classification; model evaluation; responsible use
Coming out of this section, students can: Clean, visualize, model, and evaluate a non-personal dataset and explain the limits of the result.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
14. Language Models and Applied AI







What students learn
Why it matters




Explain, use, ground, and evaluate small language-model applications responsibly.
Understanding language models helps students use, test, and evaluate artificial intelligence responsibly.



Subsections: Tokens; prediction; small models; prompting; grounding; evaluation; responsible use
Coming out of this section, students can: Build or evaluate a small grounded artificial-intelligence application with documented tests and limits.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
15. Culminating Projects







What students learn
Why it matters




Plan, build or simulate, test, revise, and explain an integrated technology project.
A culminating project combines design, construction, programming, testing, revision, and communication.



Subsections: Requirements; design; build or simulation; testing; revision; technical communication
Coming out of this section, students can: Deliver a working or simulated technology project supported by evidence, revision, and a technical explanation.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
16. Control Systems and CNC







What students learn
Why it matters




Model or build systems that use sensing, decisions, feedback, and safe states.
Control systems show how sensing, decisions, and feedback produce safe, useful machine behaviour.



Subsections: Open and closed loop control; hysteresis; proportional control; PID; interlocks; motion and CNC
Coming out of this section, students can: Model or build a feedback-controlled system with safe states, interlocks, and measured response.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
Why this is useful
Colour is easier to control when you separate what kind of colour it is from how intense and how light it is. The same model helps with screens, print, paint, and accessibility checks.

title: Understanding Colour
section: How the eye receives colour information
text:
How the eye receives colour information




A simplified eye points to the retina and optic nerve, then labels long, medium, and short wavelength cones plus rods.



Four receptor types
The guide simplifies the retina into three kinds of cone cells for colour and rod cells that are especially useful in low light.






A graph plots the overlapping response ranges of short, medium, and long wavelength cones and rods from 400 to 700 nanometres.



Overlapping responses
The curves overlap. The brain interprets a pattern of signals rather than receiving a single red, green, or blue value. Source noted in the guide.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
Separate hue, saturation, and value




Three vertical scales show hue changing through the spectrum, red losing saturation toward grey, and value changing from white to black.



Hue, saturation, value
Hue identifies the colour family. Saturation describes intensity or greyness. Value describes lightness or darkness. Source.






A colour wheel appears beside a greyscale copy. Yellow becomes very light while several blue, green, and purple hues become similar dark greys.



Different hue, similar value
Strongly different colours can have nearly the same lightness. This is why a monochrome check can reveal weak contrast. Source.

title: Understanding Colour
section: Connect the model to design software
text:
Connect the model to design software





A rainbow comparison labelled RGB on the left and CMYK on the right. The CMYK side is duller in several regions.



RGB screen, CMYK print
Screens mix emitted red, green, and blue light. Many printing systems use cyan, magenta, yellow, and black inks. A bright screen colour may reproduce with less intensity in print.






Two white rectangles cover a pink flower photograph. The high-opacity rectangle hides the flower and the low-opacity rectangle allows it to show through.



Opacity controls what shows through
High opacity blocks more of the layer below. Low opacity allows more of it to affect the result. Source noted in the guide.





Go deeper: the Munsell colour solid





A three-dimensional Munsell colour solid places value on a vertical black-to-white axis, hue around the axis, and chroma moving outward.




The Munsell system organizes colour in three dimensions: value moves vertically, hue moves around the centre, and chroma moves outward. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
Try it
Choose one hue in your design tool.

Make a vivid and a muted version by changing saturation.
Make a light and a dark version by changing value.
Convert the set to greyscale.
Record which differences remain visible without hue.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
Check your work

You can name whether you changed hue, saturation, value, or opacity.
Important colours still separate in greyscale.
You previewed a screen design on the target screen or a print design in print.
Opacity does not create an unpredictable background for text.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
Summary
Hue tells you the colour family, saturation tells you its intensity, and value tells you its lightness. Value is the most direct bridge to readable contrast. Continue to Contrast, Emphasis & Output.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
text:
Why this is useful
Type can look clear while you are zoomed in and fail at the actual size. Letter shape, spacing, line thickness, background, and output method all affect readability.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
Fonts & Text Effects
text:
Give text a reliable background




A presentation slide called Sew, Sew, Sew, Your Boat. The body text sits on a pale solid rectangle instead of directly on the changing background photograph.




The solid panel keeps the paragraph readable even when the photograph changes behind it. Example retained from the original guide.

Text placed directly on a photograph has many backgrounds at once. A solid or nearly solid panel is the most dependable fix. A shadow or outline may help a short title, but it should not be asked to rescue a paragraph.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
section: Compare effects by what they do to the letters
text:
Compare effects by what they do to the letters





Four text samples compare a thin stroke, a proper outline, an overly thick stroke, and an overly thick outline. Thick effects close spaces inside the letters.



Outline with restraint
A thin halo can separate text from a changing background. Thick effects fill counters and merge neighbouring letters. Source example.






The script word Hustle in white with a black outline and a large black drop shadow.



Shadow can separate
The outline and shadow add separation, but the script letter shapes still take longer to recognize. Style does not cancel the need to test.






The words Check it use blue 3D depth, dark outlines, highlights, curved internal strokes, and a shadow.



Effects can compete
Depth, highlights, outlines, and internal strokes all compete with the letters. Use this treatment for display only, not instructions or small labels. Source video.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
text:
Try it
Set the same short word in three fonts. Keep the size and colour identical.

View the words at 100%.
Step back or reduce the design to its final output size.
Compare the thinnest lines and the open spaces inside letters.
Add one effect at a time. Keep it only if recognition becomes faster.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
text:
Check your work

The type remains clear at the final size.
Important text does not depend on a photograph staying light or dark.
An outline does not close the spaces inside letters.
A shadow separates text without becoming a second word.
Decorative or 3D type is limited to short display text.

text:
Why this is useful
People are not the problem. A design becomes disabling when it depends on one way of seeing, reading, hearing, or operating it. Accessible design gives the same idea more than one reliable path.
For images, that second path is often text. The description should carry the image’s purpose, not list every visible object.

title: Access & Alt Text
section: Decide what kind of image it is
text:
Decide what kind of image it is


Informative
The image adds a useful fact or relationship. Write a short description of what the learner needs to notice.


Complex
The image is a chart, diagram, or detailed process. Use brief alt text and explain the important data or relationships in nearby text.


Functional
The image is a button or link. Describe the action or destination, not the way the icon looks.


Decorative
The image adds no information. Use empty alt text so a screen reader can skip it.

title: Access & Alt Text
section: Use the guide’s Google Docs example
text:
Use the guide’s Google Docs example




Google Docs with an image selected and the Image options panel open to Alt Text. The animation shows the right-click method and the Ctrl plus Alt plus Y shortcut.




The original guide demonstrates two ways to open the Alt Text control in Google Docs: right-click the image and choose Alt text, or select it and press Ctrl + Alt + Y.

Alt text is not the visible caption. A caption helps everyone understand the figure. Alt text gives an equivalent purpose or meaning when the image is unavailable.

title: Access & Alt Text
text:
Write for purpose, not pixels


Too literal
“A screenshot with a white panel, a blue square, black text, menus, and a toolbar.”


Useful
“Google Docs Image options panel open to Alt Text for a selected image.”


The useful version identifies the tool, the control, and the reason the screenshot is present. It avoids details that do not help someone complete the task.

title: Access & Alt Text
text:
Try it
Choose one instructional image from a lesson or handout.

Write one sentence stating its purpose.
Name the relationship, result, or action the learner must notice.
Remove details that do not change the meaning.
If the image is complex, add a nearby explanation that carries the full information.

title: Access & Alt Text
text:
Check your work

The description makes sense without “image of” or “picture of.”
Text shown only inside the image is available in the alt text or nearby text.
A decorative image has empty alt text.
A linked image describes where the link goes or what it does.
A complex figure has more than a one-line description somewhere on the page.

title: Access & Alt Text
text:
Summary
First decide what job the image performs. Then write the shortest text that performs the same job. Continue to Fonts & Text Effects.
Sources: W3C Images Tutorial and Harvard Digital Accessibility: Write helpful image descriptions.

title: Portable Utility-Knife Organizer
text:
Read the finished organizer

  
    
    1
    2
    3
  
  Finished prototype. The numbered markers connect the physical features to the design decisions below. Open the shared project photo.



  1Visible and easy to useAll five handles face the user. Each can be seen, counted and gripped without moving a neighbouring knife. An empty position would be obvious.
  2Portable as one objectThe tool face, side supports and base form one self-contained organizer. It can be moved to another bench without installing a permanent wall system. A carry test should still confirm that the tools remain secure while it is moved.
  3Stands on its ownThe wide base and triangular side braces create a larger footprint than the upright tool face. That support geometry helps the organizer resist tipping when a knife is removed.

title: Portable Utility-Knife Organizer
text:
Why the spacing works
Ergonomic spacing is based on the real tool and the way a person reaches for it, not only on equal distances. Each handle remains visible, the grip areas do not overlap and the outside knives have clearance from the supports. The photograph is evidence that the layout was checked with the actual utility knives.
A future test should record whether different users can remove the centre and outside knives comfortably with one hand and whether the organizer remains stable when an outside knife is removed first.

title: Portable Utility-Knife Organizer
text:
A one-sided wall version

Keep one tool face; replace the freestanding base with a French-cleat interface
If the organizer only needed tools on one side, a later version could remove the second working face and the bench base. A solid backer on the remaining tool face could engage a continuous French cleat fixed to the wall. A lower spacer would keep the organizer parallel to the wall, and an anti-lift feature would prevent it from being knocked upward during use.
This is a design direction, not a tested claim. The cleat, backer, wall, fasteners, tool load and removal forces must be built and load-tested together. Mounting hardware must suit the actual wall and load.
Browse French-cleat starting points in the Laser-Cut Gallery

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
section: Choose the support by the force path
text:
Choose the support by the force path

Straight tabbed pair: locates two members in the front plane. It still needs a separate base that provides front-to-back depth.
Angled tabbed pair: spreads the feet sideways in the front view. It still needs a separate base or rear support for front-to-back stability.
Triangular side cheeks: can carry a plaque between two side panels, but this generator does not create the required joints.
Wide single easel back: generates a T-shaped support plus optional mating-slot geometry. A fixed slot connection is not the same as a hinge.
Narrow hinged rear strut: is one component of a picture-frame-style easel. It needs a front plaque, pivot hardware and a tether or stop.
Interlocking X-base: generates two half-slotted base bars only. The upright and plaque connection must be designed separately.

The purple coupon tests the chosen tab length and calculated slot width. Blue slot rectangles are mating geometry to position in the holder plate, not separate finished parts.

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
section: Which reference file do I use?
text:
Which reference file do I use?
The SVG, DXF, DWG, CDR, PDF and PNG in the reference folder are different formats of the same template set. Do not combine all six files.

Use SVG in Inkscape. This is the easiest editable version for the laser workflow.
Use DXF or DWG in CAD/CAM software when that program handles those formats better.
Use CDR only in CorelDRAW.
Use PDF or PNG to look at or print the design. They are reference views, not the preferred editable cut file.

The external sheet contains several easel concepts. Select one complete matching group of parts, move that group into a new document, confirm the scale, and resize every slot for the measured sheet thickness. The reference was drawn around 0.118-inch material, which is slightly thinner than nominal 1/8-inch material. Always test one joint first.

title: Pill-Bottle Organizer | Five Reference Assemblies
text:
Bill-of-material and parameter routine
For any selected reference:

Measure at least three bottles: body diameter, cap diameter, height and any taper.
Choose the controlling diameter and required radial clearance.
Calculate opening = largest measured body + 2 × radial clearance.
Set centre spacing from cap diameter, hand access and remaining material, not appearance alone.
Update part dimensions and BOM before nesting.
Cut an opening coupon, record actual fit, then revise the source.
Dry-assemble; test insertion, removal, labels, tipping and collisions.

title: Pill-Bottle Organizer | Five Reference Assemblies
text:
Physical-test record
All five files currently have status unverified. Do not change that label because the SVG opens correctly. Record the material, measured thickness, machine, settings reference, date, tester, actual opening, fit result, load and revision before promoting a design to fit-tested or shop-tested.

title: Pill-Bottle Organizer | Five Reference Assemblies
text:
Reference systems worth studying
The sketches below are original Technology Commons diagrams, not copied product images. Follow each source to inspect the actual system and its licence. Borrow a principle only after checking dimensions, load, access, fabrication method and the source’s current terms.






French cleat


Principle: a continuous angled interface makes modules movable while the lower stand-off controls tilt.


Adapt: add an anti-lift or anti-slide feature where impact is possible.


Source: Wikipedia contributors · page content CC BY-SA · reference link · original schematic here is AGPL-3.0 · reference only







Gridfinity


Principle: a shared pitch lets containers move without redesigning the whole storage field.


Adapt: use a consistent centre spacing or interface datum across shop modules.


Source: Zack Freedman / Voidstar Lab and Kenneth Hodson’s rebuild · MIT · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







openGrid


Principle: a regular wall field separates the mounting interface from each accessory.


Adapt: document one interface and test light- and heavy-duty versions separately.


Source: David D / openGrid contributors · core parts CC BY · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







Pegstr


Principle: parametric holders begin with the object and the host-board standard.


Adapt: measure both; do not assume imported inch pegboard dimensions match local stock.


Source: MGX3D · CC BY-NC · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







5S shadow board


Principle: a visible home position makes missing or misplaced items obvious.


Adapt: labels and silhouettes should support return, counting and inspection, not decoration.


Source: National Highways visual-management standard · Crown publication, linked for reference; no source media reused · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







Flexible fabrication workshop


Principle: organize around workflow, shared infrastructure and reconfigurable work zones.


Adapt: map where material arrives, work happens, parts wait and completed work leaves.


Source: Open Source Ecology contributors · open-source project; linked page terms govern reuse and no source media is copied · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only









Warning



Wall mounting is not a decorative SVG problem. The wall substrate, anchor, fastener, backer, load, impact and inspection routine must be approved by the responsible instructor. A laser-cut plate is not a rated anchor.

Printables, Thingiverse, and MakerWorld are useful for studying retention, mounting, modularity, adjustment, and fabrication choices. Check the licence on each model.

Original sketches are preferred. If a teacher-approved vector reference is used, record the creator, original page, licence and changes made. Use public-domain, open-licensed or otherwise permitted work; a search result thumbnail or “free SVG” label is not enough.

title: Holiday Ornament / Reindeer | Compact Laser Project
Holiday Ornament / Reindeer | Compact Laser Project
text:
Evaluate
Check silhouette, readable personalization, surface finish, hanging balance, fragile features, material use and whether the final work still respects its source licence. Record one change for a future version.
Return to Laser Cutting & 2D Fabrication or find open starting geometry in the Laser Fabrication Library.

text: Identify a genuine need in the classroom, shop, school, home, or community. Use the full N.I.C.E. cycle to design, communicate, fabricate, test, and improve a response. The process may include laser cutting, but the selected materials and processes must follow from the need.

title: Design & Fabrication Capstone | Complete a N.I.C.E. Design Cycle
text: Identify a genuine need in the classroom, shop, school, home, or community. Use the full N.I.C.E. cycle to design, communicate, fabricate, test, and improve a response. The process may include laser cutting, but the selected materials and processes must follow from the need.

title: Design & Fabrication Capstone | Complete a N.I.C.E. Design Cycle
text:
Required design record

Situation and need: user, context, facts, assumptions, requirements, restrictions, necessities, and priorities.
Inquiry: useful questions, credible sources, existing solutions, comparisons, and opportunities to borrow, combine, adapt, or improve.
Alternatives: distinct concepts with reasons, not cosmetic variations of one idea.
Selected concept: labelled communication, dimensions, materials, process plan, and identified uncertainties.
Prototype: a purposeful model or test for the highest-risk question.
Fabrication: versioned files, settings, material records, safe process, and assembly decisions.
Feedback and testing: observations from realistic use, measurements, and user response.
Evaluation and iteration: evidence compared with the need and a documented next version.

title: Design & Fabrication Capstone | Complete a N.I.C.E. Design Cycle
text:
Assessment emphasis
Assess the quality of decisions, evidence, communication, responsible process use, and revision, not only the polish of the final artifact. Reward students who discover a problem early, explain it clearly, and improve the design.
Use the N.I.C.E. classroom resource collection to support the design record and the Laser Fabrication Library for editable test geometry and component starting points.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Adaptable to TIJ1O and to project-based expectations in TDJ, TMJ, TCJ, TTJ, TEJ, and TGJ where the chosen need, design communication, materials, processes, and testing authentically fit the course.

Continue with the planned 3D Printing and Additive Manufacturing module, or begin another N.I.C.E. iteration.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Use the process that best suits each function. Thin laser-cut Baltic birch is valuable for precision faces, tool openings, slots, holes, dividers, shadow-board fronts, engraved labels, retainers, spacers, alignment aids, and drilling templates. It is not automatically the right structural rail or load-bearing backer.
Use 1/2 inch or 3/4 inch plywood, conventional lumber, commercial fasteners, dowels, or other approved materials where stiffness, impact resistance, screw holding, or load capacity matters.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Use the process that best suits each function. Thin laser-cut Baltic birch is valuable for precision faces, tool openings, slots, holes, dividers, shadow-board fronts, engraved labels, retainers, spacers, alignment aids, and drilling templates. It is not automatically the right structural rail or load-bearing backer.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Assembly vocabulary

Floor and walls: establish the main volume and load path.
Tabs and slots: locate parts and transfer forces when sized for actual material.
Pins and dowels: align, hinge, retain, or reinforce.
Screws: allow removable mechanical assembly when the receiving material is suitable.
Glue: bonds compatible surfaces but should not compensate for a poorly fitted or unsafe structure.
Spacers and laminations: create controlled offsets or thicker local features.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Hybrid template strategy
A laser-cut face can act as a drilling or placement template for a thicker plywood backer. Clamp the template safely, locate holes accurately, transfer the pattern, then attach the precision face to the structural part. This preserves repeatability without pretending a thin sheet should carry every load.
Use joinery and French-cleat components as measured starting points and validate every interface physically.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Strong connections to TMJ2O, TCJ2O, TDJ2O, and TIJ1O through material selection, assemblies, joinery, fasteners, manufacturing planning, prototyping, and evaluation.

Next: apply these decisions to a useful holder using the Tool Organizer Gallery and design criteria.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text: Create a simple holder for measured classroom objects such as markers, pencils, screwdrivers, drill bits, or small electronics tools. The openings must come from real measurements, not a generic file or guessed diameter.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text: Create a simple holder for measured classroom objects such as markers, pencils, screwdrivers, drill bits, or small electronics tools. The openings must come from real measurements, not a generic file or guessed diameter.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text:
Measure the object
Use calipers correctly and record units. Measure more than one example when nominally identical objects may vary. Identify the controlling dimension: outside diameter, widest body, collar, taper, handle shape, or removal clearance.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text:
Build the layout

Create one opening from an exact measured dimension.
Decide what clearance the task requires; do not silently treat a nominal measurement as a finished fit.
Duplicate the opening into a controlled row or array.
Set centre-to-centre spacing and edge margins numerically.
Align labels and openings consistently.
Check that the remaining material between openings is strong enough for the intended use.

Use circles, holes, slots, rulers, and spacing templates as editable references. The source geometry is a starting point; the student’s measured object determines the final design.
For the first controlled organizer exercise, compare the Hole, Slot and Organizer palettes. Copy named groups, enter dimensions numerically, and make every repeated opening from one checked original.
Draw front, top and side views on the planning worksheet before building the digital layout. Use the Paper-to-Inkscape workflow for datums, grouping, alignment and preflight.
For a row, grid, staggered, radial or perimeter layout, the Fabrication Plate Builder can turn the checked measurements into a reproducible true-size SVG. It validates boundaries and overlap, but the calibration lesson is still required to decide the finished fit.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text:
Evidence
Submit a measurement table, dimensioned layout, fabrication file, fit observation, and one revision. A visually even layout is not enough if tools bind, fall through, or cannot be removed easily.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Useful for TIJ1O, TMJ2O, TDJ2O, TCJ2O, TEJ2O, and TTJ2O contexts involving measurement, precision, layout, repeated geometry, tool organization, and prototype evaluation.

Next: learn why the measured opening and the cut result can differ in Material Fit + Calibration.

text:
Why this is useful
The tutorial showed you where the tools are and how they work. A designer must also make choices. This project asks you to use the same basic steps with your own name, your own logo, and your own layout.
You are designing for a real object. Good spacing, readable letters, and clean files make the name tag easier to understand and easier to manufacture.






ImportantThis is the task after the Andrade tutorial



Finish Photopea Lesson 3 and its video first. The ANDRADE file is a worked example, not your submission. Save a new copy and replace the example with your own design.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
Design brief
Create an original name tag for a teacher-approved 11 × 4 inch blank. Put a personal logo in the left area and your name in the remaining space. The name must be readable from about 2 metres away. Keep everything away from the edges and prepare clean files for teacher approval.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
What you will submit
Submit these three versions of the same design:

PSD: the editable master with clearly named layers.
PNG: a transparent preview or engraving image at 3300 × 1200 pixels.
SVG: the vector version with the logo and name visible.

Use clear filenames:

studentnumber-lastname-name-tag-master.psd
studentnumber-lastname-name-tag.png
studentnumber-lastname-name-tag.svg

Every filename must begin with your student number, followed by your last name. Replace studentnumber and lastname with your own information. Example: 123456789-Smith-name-tag-master.psd.
Your teacher will tell you which file the machine workflow needs. A PNG can be used for raster engraving. An SVG can carry paths for scoring, cutting, plotting, or another fabrication process.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag

2. Compare three ideas
These three versions use the same name and logo. Look at all three before choosing.



1. Large first letter



Technology Commons emblem beside large A. ANDRADE text.


The first letter is large, but the name takes longer to read.



2. Chosen: simple and clear



Small Technology Commons emblem beside extra-large ANDRADE text.


I chose this version because the full name is easier to read.

Technology Commons emblem, thick AA lettermark, and large NDRADE text.


The AA makes the design more personal, but it makes the name harder to read.

Which version can you read fastest?
What do you notice first?
Is there enough empty space?

Simple is easier to read. The Commons logo and the full name are both clear.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag

3. Make a new working copy

Open your completed file from Photopea Lesson 3.
Choose File > Save as PSD immediately.
Give the copy your own filename.
Keep the canvas at 11 × 4 inches and 300 pixels per inch.
Keep the background transparent.
Add a 0.25 inch safe margin on every side.

At 300 pixels per inch, the document is 3300 × 1200 pixels and the 0.25 inch margin is 75 pixels.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
4. Try fonts before choosing
Type your own name in at least three fonts. Keep the examples at the same size so you can compare them fairly.



The name Andrade shown in four font styles: balanced sans serif, serif, heavy and narrow, and script.


Choose the version that is easy to read in two seconds, has open letter shapes, and is thick enough to engrave. Do not stretch the letters to make them fit.






TipQuick test



Show the three versions to another person for two seconds. Use the one they can read first, unless another choice has a strong reason.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
5. Replace the example logo
Use the logo you traced in Lesson 2 or another teacher-approved personal mark.

Place the SVG or transparent PNG on its own layer.
Keep the width-and-height link turned on.
Resize from a corner so the logo does not stretch.
Keep the logo inside the left 4 × 4 inch area.
Leave visible space around the logo.

If your logo replaces the first letter of your name, check that the complete word is still obvious. Match the logo’s thickness and baseline to the letters.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
6. Make the layout look intentional
Check the complete design, not one layer at a time:

Safe margin: nothing crosses the 0.25 inch guide.
Logo area: the logo stays in the left 4 × 4 inch space.
Alignment: the logo and name feel centred from top to bottom.
Gap: the logo and name are connected but do not collide.
Hierarchy: your name is the first or equal reading target.
Balance: the empty space on one side does not make the design feel as if it is falling over.
Distance: the name is readable from about 2 metres away.




Small Technology Commons emblem beside extra-large ANDRADE text.


The simple version works best because the full name is easy to read.
Hide the guides and ask another person what they notice first. If they cannot read the name in two seconds, revise the size, font, spacing, or logo.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:

PSD

Keep the text and logo editable.
Name important layers.
Save the full 11 × 4 inch document.



PNG

Hide the background and guides.
Export at 3300 × 1200 pixels.
Reopen the file and check its transparency, spelling, and crop.



SVG

Export with raster graphics turned off.
Reopen the SVG and check that the complete design appears.







WarningCheck the SVG before submitting



Photopea may leave a placed SVG smart object out of an SVG export. If the logo disappears, open the logo SVG, copy its vector layers, paste those layers into the name-tag file, hide the smart-object copy, and export again.

A vertical guide marks four inches from the left side of the transparent nameplate.

3. Type the name

Select the Type Tool (T).
