The name Andrade added to the right side of the nameplate.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
4. Try several fonts
Select the whole name. Try at least three fonts before choosing one. Change only the font at first. This makes the choices easier to compare.
Try:

a serif font;
a decorative or rounded font; and
a plain sans serif font.

A serif font has small finishing strokes on the letters. Serif fonts are common in printed books. A sans serif font does not have those strokes. Sans serif fonts are often a clearer starting point for signs and nameplates.
   
No font is always good or bad. The best font fits the job and stays easy to read.

Serif: try Georgia or Times New Roman for a printed-book look. Check the thin strokes.
Sans serif: try DejaVu Sans, Arial, Verdana, or Open Sans for clear letters.
Rounded or display: try Nunito, Montserrat, or Impact for personality. Check for crowding.
Script or decorative: use joined or detailed letters with care. They can be hard to read and engrave.

Font names may vary. Choose a similar font if one is unavailable.



Andrade shown in a serif font while the student compares font choices.


Ask these questions:

Can I read the name quickly?
Can I tell similar characters apart, such as I, l, and 1?
Are the lines thick enough to engrave?
Do the spaces inside a, e, and o stay open?

Read the name from an arm’s length away. If you need extra time to recognize it, try a simpler font.
Zoom out until the whole nameplate fits on the screen. Compare the fonts again at the smaller view. The Accessible Design guide shows why this test matters.
The example ends with DejaVu Sans Book at about 300 px. Another clear sans serif font is also fine.

A need is something the solution must address. Requirements and restrictions are conditions the solution has to work within.

Necessities are required for the solution to work. Nice-to-haves could improve the solution but are not required.




Necessities


Nice-to-haves

text:
6. Most important needs
Choose the needs that matter most before you begin Inquiry.




Priority need


Why it matters most

title: User Needs
text:
7. Need statement
Complete this in one or two sentences:

The user needs ___ because ___ while considering ___.

“We need a laser-cut name tag” already chooses the product. “A new classmate needs to identify who they are speaking with quickly and from a useful distance” keeps the problem open.

title: User Needs

What did you learn or make?
What evidence shows that your work is complete and correct?
What will you improve next time?

title: Rank the Priorities
text: I can rank nice-to-haves and explain which improvements should guide the design first.

title: Rank the Priorities
text: I can rank nice-to-haves and explain which improvements should guide the design first.

title: Rank the Priorities
text:
Use the 1-10 scale

10: necessity; the design fails without it.
7-9: high-value improvement.
4-6: useful improvement.
1-3: minor preference.

Give each nice-to-have a score and one short reason. Do not give every item a 9. Ranking only helps when it shows real trade-offs.

title: Rank the Priorities
text:
Compare two ideas
Check every idea against all necessities first. Then compare how well each idea addresses the highest-ranked nice-to-haves. The score supports a decision; it does not replace judgement or user feedback.
Complete the priorities section of the N.I.C.E. Needs Worksheet.

title: Investigate & Inquire
text:
Go wide, then investigate
Brainstorm several different possibilities before researching. Use quick sketches, changed materials, different orientations, and borrow, combine, adapt, improve prompts.
Then ask four questions:

What do we need?
What already exists?
What could work for us?
What would we change?

Record what is good, what is a problem, and what still needs to be checked. Name the sources you used.
Use the N.I.C.E. Inquiry Worksheet.

title: Evaluate, Improve & Repeat
text:
Compare evidence with the plan
Check the original situation, facts, assumptions, user needs, necessities, and ranked nice-to-haves. Group repeated feedback into patterns instead of obeying every individual comment.
For each important part, choose:

Keep: evidence shows it works.
Change: evidence points to a specific improvement.
Remove: it adds complexity without enough value.
Test: there is not enough evidence yet.

Finish this sentence: The evidence changes our understanding of , so the next cycle will .
Use the N.I.C.E. Evaluate Worksheet.

title: Land Lettermark
text:
The design jam
Combine three things:

one of your initials;
one careful observation of land, water, light, roots, paths, texture, or movement; and
one Good Life value that matters to you.

title: Land Lettermark
text:
Observe before drawing
Go outside and record three specific observations. Slow down. Observe or photograph, leave living things in place, and notice relationships such as water and soil, roots and paths, or light and shadow.

title: Land Lettermark
text:
Sketch three options
Make three quick lettermarks. Change the shape, spacing, direction, or relationship between the letter and the observation. Notice the approach of Indigenous artists without copying an artist’s style or cultural symbols.
Beside your strongest sketch, write:

Value: the idea you want the mark to carry;
Land observation: what you noticed; and
Design choice: how the shape communicates both.

title: Iteration 1: Robert Abraham and the CNC Lathe
text:
Mr. Knowles used to joke that my cohort was “Iteration 1”, the first group through the program. Many of us went on to engineering at Waterloo, U of T, and elsewhere.
This year, my own Iteration 1 has graduated and started university. I want to record some of what they accomplished, especially for anyone looking for co-op students, interns, or part-time technical help.
The important context for these stories is that this was not simply the assigned course work. These students did the regular work, did it to a high standard, and then chose problems that interested them and went much further. The best description is probably an impressive engineering side quest: the main quest was already complete.

title: Iteration 1: Robert Abraham and the CNC Lathe
text:
Robert Abraham
Introducing Robert Abraham, now studying Computer Engineering at the University of Toronto. You can find more about him and his projects at robert-abraham.com/projects.
Our school offers a Specialist High Skills Major (SHSM) in Manufacturing, and Computer Engineering is one of the elective courses students can take as part of that program. One of the goals is to connect those two worlds more deliberately: electronics, controls, programming, and Linux meeting machining, fabrication, and real manufacturing systems.
In Grade 11 Computer Engineering, Robert took the initiative to work on an old Lab-Volt CNC lathe that another high school was going to throw out. Restoring it was not an assigned project. He saw a difficult, open-ended problem and decided to take it on. Before Christmas, we were already machining our first part: a Christmas tree. Here is how it happened.



Disassembling the old Lab-Volt CNC lathe as we worked through its mechanical problems.


When we opened the electronics cabinet, the wiring was difficult to trace and did not consistently follow convention, including black being used as positive on part of the DC circuit.



Inside the CNC lathe electronics cabinet while we traced the existing system and planned the retrofit.


Robert researched a replacement controller compatible with the existing Gecko drives, and we worked through the electrical and mechanical problems. The mechanical work meant disassembling parts of the machine, cleaning them, resolving issues, and putting everything back together.
The broken controller was the only component we had to replace. Everything else was done using what we already had, open-source software, or software available free through student educational access.
We ran the machine with LinuxCNC, so part of the retrofit meant setting up and configuring our own Linux-based controller computer and operating system. LinuxCNC gave us an open-source machine-control platform without needing to buy proprietary CNC control software.



The rebuilt lathe running from our LinuxCNC controller computer.


We did not have another Mastercam licence available either. Robert learned Autodesk Inventor through educational access, generated the G-code, and kept pushing until the machine ran a program.



The finished CNC lathe after the retrofit and rebuild.


That project is a good example of what I want computer engineering to be: not just following instructions, but inheriting a broken system, researching what you do not know, and making it work. The impressive part was not that Robert completed an assignment. It was that he chose to go well beyond one.
Posted with Robert’s permission. If you are looking for an intern, co-op student, or someone for part-time technical work, consider reaching out to him.
Robert Abraham’s projects: robert-abraham.com/projects

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
Start with community
Moon teachings are not identical across First Nations. Names, spellings, timing, and meanings change with language, territory, family, and community.
The sequence below comes from a Matawa Education and Care Centre resource, which identifies these as the 13 Moons of the Mississaugas of the Credit. Port Credit Secondary School stands within the traditional territory of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation.
The local sources use Grandmother Moon, rather than Mother Moon. A Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation notice names her Tibik Giizis Nookmissmaan and connects Grandmother Moon with water, cleansing, gratitude, and intention. See page 11 of the November 2019 Eaglepress.






Note



This page is a starting point, not a replacement for an Elder, Knowledge Keeper, language speaker, or community teacher.

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
Read the turtle’s back





A common snapping turtle swimming at Toronto’s Evergreen Brick Works.


A living turtle. Photograph by Maxquijano at Toronto’s Evergreen Brick Works, 2011, CC BY-SA 3.0.





A photographed turtle-shell calendar display with 13 large centre sections.


A material example. Iroquoian turtle-shell calendar display at the Droulers-Tsiionhiakwatha archaeological site. Photograph by Pierre5018, 2020, CC BY-SA 4.0. The photographed edge has 25 visible small sections, which is why this page treats the numbers as a teaching pattern rather than a universal anatomy test.



What to notice


13large centre sectionsthe Grandmother Moons


28small edge marksdays in the teaching cycle


The Oneida Language and Cultural Centre explains the same 13-and-28 relationship. A Mississaugas of the Credit classroom story describes children counting 13 spots and connecting them to the 13 Moons. See page 14 of the May 2026 Eaglepress.

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
The 13 Grandmother Moons
These compact meanings summarize the Mississaugas of the Credit sequence in the Matawa resource. Gregorian months are approximate guides, not fixed start and end dates.


1 · January

Mnido Giizis


Spirit Moon

quiet reflection


2 · February

Makwa Giizis


Bear Moon

birth and reflection


3 · March

Ziissbaakdoke Giizis


Sugar Moon

maple sap runs


4 · April

Namebine Giizis


Sucker Moon

fish return and sustain


5 · May

Waawaaskone Giizis


Flower Moon

flowers and medicines grow


6 · June

Odemin Giizis


Strawberry Moon

healing and reconciliation


7 · July

Mskomini Giizis


Raspberry Moon

gentleness and kindness


8 · July to August

Datkaamin Giizis


Blackberry or Thimbleberry Moon

a less frequent harvest


9 · August

Mdaamiin Giizis


Corn Moon

future generations


10 · September

Biinaakwe Giizis


Falling Leaves Moon

Creation gives back


11 · October

Mshkawji Giizis


Freezing Moon

prepare for winter


12 · November

Mnidoons Giizis Oonhg


Little Spirit Moon

healing and a good path


13 · December

Mnidoons Giizis


Blue or Big Spirit Moon

purification and healing


Other Anishinaabe communities may use different names, spellings, orders, or teachings because the land and community are different.

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
New Moon and Old Moon


🌘

Old Moon


The thin waning crescent shortly before New Moon. This is an informal sky-watching name, not one of the 13 Grandmother Moon names.



🌑

New Moon


An astronomical phase when the lit side faces mostly away from Earth. The visible crescent grows afterward.



See NASA’s Moon phases guide for the complete astronomical sequence.

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
Keep the two measures clear


13Grandmother Moonsa seasonal teaching round


28teaching daysshown around the shell


29.5astronomical daysabout one New Moon to the next


The turtle-shell teaching carries relationship, memory, and seasonal meaning. Astronomical measurement describes orbital timing. NASA gives about 27.3 days for one orbit around Earth and 29.5 days from one New Moon to the next.

text:
Citation style
References use stable numbering based on the IEEE Reference Guide. A page can cite a whole source as [1] or a specific location as [1, Ch. 3, p. 76] or [1, Ch. 3, pp. 76–84].
For classroom use, this site modifies the usual IEEE locator by including the textbook chapter number whenever it is known. Chapter numbers make the cited material easier for students to find when they buy or use an edition whose page numbers differ.
As additional sources are added, their reference numbers remain stable so existing citations do not need to be rewritten.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
I teach and learn Technological Education at Port Credit Secondary School. Teaching is more than content: knowledge helps us build skill, judgement, and practical wisdom so we can grow in capability, live well, and learn through experience. This site shares lessons, assignments, slides, experiments, and revisions so others can adapt them, learn by doing, and follow the way in their own work.
The resources are organized around Ontario’s Technological Education curriculum, with connections to other curricular and co-curricular learning where they are useful. Across the courses, the resources also connect with Port Credit’s SciTech Regional Program and can support Ontario’s Specialist High Skills Major (SHSM) in Manufacturing, including sector-focused learning, certifications, experiential learning, career exploration, reach-ahead experiences, and sector-partnered experiences.








NoteWork in progress and public contributions



This site is a living collection of teaching materials. It may contain errors, omissions, outdated information, and areas with significant room for improvement. If you find something that can be corrected or improved, please open an issue or submit a pull request.
The GitHub repository, issues, pull requests, comments, and commit history are public. Do not post student information, personal information, confidential school or board information, account information, or other sensitive material. Review and redact your contribution before publishing it. Contributors are responsible for the information they choose to place in a public GitHub contribution; this project cannot protect information that someone has chosen to publish publicly.




Before teaching at Port Credit, I worked at Palantir, ran a startup called PetroPredict, and completed internships at Facebook, Suncor, and several smaller technology companies. Earlier, while I was still in high school, I worked as a lifeguard and deck supervisor with the City of Mississauga and in a machine shop after a co-op placement.
Outside work and school, I was a sponsored kiteboarder for Switch Kites and have been an avid box lacrosse player. Kiteboarding was a major part of my life and shaped how I think about practice, judgement, risk, feedback, equipment, weather, failure, and learning from people who have different skills, knowledge, and wisdom from you.



After moving back to Mississauga following time living abroad, kiteboarding became something I could realistically do only a few times a year. I needed other ways to keep learning with people, contributing to communities, and doing things that require practice.
I now volunteer, guest speak, and run workshops with a variety of organizations, but I spend the most time contributing to my local parish in Mississauga. I am of Goan Catholic heritage, and I have helped with children’s programs including First Holy Communion and with liturgy involving exceptional individuals.
I take my own beliefs seriously while also trying to study other philosophies and religious traditions with respect. That helps me understand more of the people I teach and work with, and gives me more ways to think about learning, discipline, community, service, attention, and human well-being. More recently, I have been training in Gong Fu and Qigong with the Chung Wah Kung Fu International System and the Human Wellness and Recuperation Centre.



The goal is simple: useful teaching and learning material is open-source, free to access, and easy to adapt. Learners, educators, and anyone else who can use it can access basic knowledge without a paywall or dependence on a single classroom, platform, or account.
This approach is influenced by open education projects such as Tony R. Kuphaldt’s Socratic Electronics, which emphasizes learning through questions, research, discussion, explaining ideas to others, and developing the ability to teach yourself.
The material here is meant to be used, questioned, adapted, improved, and shared again.



Many religions and philosophies contain ideas that can sound similar, much as versions of the Golden Rule appear across different traditions. Similarity does not make them identical. I do not want to flatten distinct histories, beliefs, languages, or practices into one system. These are short ideas I find useful to keep nearby when thinking about teaching, learning, practice, and community.

The Way: I use the Way here in a broad, non-doctrinal sense: being present with things as they are, without judgement, and letting the path become clearer through practice. The focus is on being rather than constantly reaching for the next outcome: doing one thing mindfully, acting effectively, accepting what is present, and working without attachment to a particular result. This also connects to well-being as something lived and practised across the physical, mental, spiritual, and emotional parts of a person. Different traditions use the idea of a way or path differently, and those differences matter.
Spirit: Spirit can describe something carried within a person, but also something strengthened between people: school spirit, team spirit, community spirit. It can grow through belonging, responsibility, shared effort, service, and the feeling that your work is connected to something larger than yourself.
Paul Cormier / Indigenous learning methodology: Kinoo’amaadawaad Megwaa Doodamawaad, translated by Cormier as “they are learning with each other while they are doing.” I want that idea to shape these notes: students learn with one another while doing real work, and the documentation grows from that work.
Confucianism: learn something, then practise it. Learning is not complete when something has merely been heard or read.
Daoism: a long journey begins beneath your feet. Large work starts from what is small and present, and care at the end matters as much as enthusiasm at the beginning.
Stoicism: Epictetus treats education as more than book knowledge; character and judgement are developed through repeated practice and self-correction.
Epicureanism: Epicurus places unusual weight on friendship as part of a good life. Learning is easier to sustain when people enjoy doing worthwhile things together.
Hindu tradition: the Bhagavad Gita 2:47 distinguishes action from attachment to its results: do the work carefully without letting the outcome become the only reason for doing it.
Buddhism: the Dhammapada 76 compares a wise person who points out your faults to someone revealing hidden treasure. Good correction can be a gift.
Jewish tradition: Pirkei Avot 4:1 asks, “Who is wise?” and answers: the person who learns from every person.
Christian tradition: “Iron sharpens iron” is a useful image for people improving one another through honest contact, practice, challenge, and care.
Islamic learning tradition: “Seek knowledge from the cradle to the grave” is a widely repeated educational maxim. It is worth carrying for its meaning, while being careful not to present it as a verified Prophetic hadith. The Qur’an also gives the concise prayer, “My Lord, increase me in knowledge”.
Ubuntu: “A person is a person through other persons.” The idea of umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu keeps learning connected to relationship, dignity, and community.
“Each one, teach one.” Knowledge becomes more useful when it moves through people instead of stopping with the first person who receives it.
OSSTF/FEESO: “Let us not take thought for our separate interests, but let us help one another.”
Port Credit: Lux numquam desit. Let light never be lacking. The light is something we keep alive for one another: showing up, sharing what we know, helping each other forward, and carrying the Way on.

The common thread is not that these traditions are identical. It is that many very different traditions take practice, humility, relationship, disciplined attention, service, and lifelong learning seriously.
The religious, spiritual, philosophical, and cultural references above describe ideas I study and influences I find useful. They are not belief requirements for students. Students are not expected to adopt, reject, defend, or disclose a religious, spiritual, Indigenous, philosophical, or non-religious belief. Classroom reflection can remain secular and can use interests, projects, community, culture, technical work, or another non-sensitive point of reference. Agreement with a belief is never assessed.

This site is partly an attempt to continue a tradition I benefited from long before I became a teacher: educators making useful material available to people they may never meet.
Michael Franzen maintained a site that was extremely useful to me during teachers college. That site is now offline, but the example stayed with me: a teacher could put useful technical material on the open web and someone outside their classroom could learn from it.
Peter Beens has likewise shared a substantial body of educational and technical material through peter.beens.ca, beens.org, and Beens Consulting.
I also owe a great deal to the technology team at Westdale Secondary School, who shared an enormous amount of material, experience, and practical advice:

Taylor Wilson: computer and transportation technology
Dave Kipp: construction and woodworking
David Christie: mathematics, science, and general technology
Craig Ramsden: construction and woodworking
Rejean Royer: transportation technology
Principal Brian Goodram

The wooden MR. ANDRADE name tag shown in this project was made and gifted to me by teachers at Westdale. Rejean also shared with me parts of his Indigenous heritage and his practice of smudging as part of his daily life. I am grateful for the trust involved in sharing both technical knowledge and personal tradition.
This project is meant to carry that spirit forward: take what is useful, credit the people who helped, improve it where you can, and leave something behind for the next person.



This project currently reflects my classroom work and the people whose ideas, feedback, and resources have influenced it. As others contribute directly to the site, contributor bios will be added here.
LinkedIn · GitHub · Personal site



Technological Education Resources is built for teaching at Port Credit Secondary School, and its visual identity deliberately connects to the school without trying to replace the school’s own identity.
Port Credit’s secondary-school history reaches back to 1919, when a continuation school opened in the community. The PCSS Alumni Association preserves school history, yearbooks, memorabilia, and stories while supporting scholarships and selected school projects.
The Regional SciTech Program launched in September 2005. Alumni material describes it as an integrated science and technology program intended for both inquiry-oriented academic learners and hands-on learners interested in college, apprenticeships, skilled trades, and industry.
The school motto, Lux numquam desit, is a natural fit for a visual system built around the Port Credit lighthouse, learning, and the idea of carrying useful knowledge forward.
Technological Education Resources also recognizes the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation and the Indigenous history and continuing stewardship connected to this place. Purple and orange are included in the working palette as community and reflection accents that can be used thoughtfully in Indigenous learning and reconciliation contexts. They are project colours, not presented as official colours of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation.

Mindfulness and well-being activities on this site are educational classroom practices, not therapy, counselling, diagnosis, or mental-health treatment. They may appear as brief start-up activities, pauses, check-ins, or reflections that support attention, self-regulation, readiness to learn, reflection, and awareness of physical, mental, spiritual, and emotional well-being. They sit alongside and around the curriculum as part of the learning environment rather than as therapeutic assignments.
These activities fit the promotion end of PDSB’s tiered mental-health model. PDSB’s 2026-2029 Mental Health and Addictions Strategy describes Tier 1 as positive mental-health and well-being promotion for all students through inclusive learning environments, social-emotional learning, and stigma reduction. Specialized consultation, assessment, family support, and therapeutic services sit at Tier 3 with appropriate mental-health professionals. The public PDSB Mental Health and Well-Being page is the starting point for current board resources and pathways to care.
Students are not asked to diagnose themselves or others, disclose private mental-health information, or participate in therapy as coursework. Personal disclosure, emotional intensity, or the private details of a student’s life are not a basis for assessment. Where reflection is assessed, the evidence is the curriculum learning or observable learning process identified in the task, not a student’s mental-health status or willingness to reveal personal information.


If a student asks for mental-health help, or a concern moves beyond ordinary classroom support, the role moves from classroom learning to connection and referral. Depending on the situation, that pathway can include Guidance or Student Services, school administration, the School Support Team, PDSB social work or psychology services, parents or caregivers, and community or regulated health professionals. PDSB’s current strategy calls for clear pathways to both school and community supports.
The teacher’s role is to notice, listen, respond appropriately, maintain professional boundaries, reduce stigma, and connect students with the people whose role and training fit the concern. It does not include diagnosing a condition or providing treatment. This reflects the Ontario College of Teachers’ Supporting Students’ Mental Health advisory, including its direction to observe, listen, inform, and involve others rather than counsel outside the educator’s role and training.
Students are not promised absolute confidentiality. When safety, suspected abuse or neglect, self-harm, threats, or another reporting obligation is involved, applicable school and board procedures, emergency protocols, and the OCT Duty to Report advisory govern the response. Professional relationships and communications also follow the OCT Professional Boundaries advisory and the Professional Standards.




AI can be used as an iterative learning partner for activities such as brainstorming, inquiry, coding, accessibility, drafting, feedback, and reflection on process when the task permits it. It does not replace professional judgement or reliable evidence of student learning. Assignment-specific directions identify what AI assistance is permitted and how it is attributed. Students may be asked to retain prompts and relevant outputs as evidence of process, while keeping personal and sensitive information out of those prompts.
Confidential or sensitive student information is not entered into public or unapproved AI tools. This includes student names or numbers, school account information, identifiable student work, grades, IEP or accommodation information, health or mental-health information, family circumstances, images or recordings, and other personal information. Student-facing third-party software use follows current PDSB approval, privacy, age, notice, and consent requirements.
PDSB’s published 2023 interim guidance on Artificial Intelligence in Education emphasizes transparency, privacy, verification of AI output, attribution, protection of confidential student data, and caution with AI-detection tools. Because AI tools, approvals, and board requirements change, current PDSB approved-tool, privacy, and instructional requirements take precedence over that interim document. The PDSB Privacy and Terms page provides the board’s public privacy information. Ontario’s O. Reg. 52/26, in force July 1, 2026, also requires school-board notice when student personal digital information is disclosed to qualifying third-party software applications.
AI-generated or AI-assisted educational material is reviewed for factual accuracy, context, bias, accessibility, privacy, and copyright before use. AI-detection output is not treated as proof by itself.



This site publishes generic teaching resources, not student records or routine student submissions. Student names, student numbers, contact information, grades, IEP or accommodation information, health information, and other private student data remain in board-approved systems. Identifiable student work, images, stories, or recordings are published only when the applicable permission, consent, and board requirements have been addressed.



Documents on this site are not safety documentation and are not to be used as a substitute for safety instruction, safety procedures, certification, supervision, authorization, or official safety requirements. I intend to avoid publishing stand-alone safety procedures here.
For safety documentation and procedures, use current authoritative sources appropriate to the actual activity and equipment. These include the Ontario Council for Technology Education (OCTE) Safety resources, your own school board and school safety procedures, employer requirements where applicable, manufacturer manuals and instructions, safety data sheets, applicable legislation and standards, and other official resources required for the setting.
Where a task involves tools, machinery, electrical systems, batteries, vehicles, lifting, fabrication, chemicals, heat, or another hazard, the current official procedure for the actual equipment and environment governs.



Technological Education Resources is an independently maintained collection of teaching materials, not a substitute for official PDSB, school, Ministry of Education, Ontario College of Teachers, or legal requirements. Where a resource conflicts with a current official requirement, the current official requirement governs.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
I teach and learn Technological Education at Port Credit Secondary School. Teaching is more than content: knowledge helps us build skill, judgement, and practical wisdom so we can grow in capability, live well, and learn through experience. This site shares lessons, assignments, slides, experiments, and revisions so others can adapt them, learn by doing, and follow the way in their own work.
The resources are organized around Ontario’s Technological Education curriculum, with connections to other curricular and co-curricular learning where they are useful. Across the courses, the resources also connect with Port Credit’s SciTech Regional Program and can support Ontario’s Specialist High Skills Major (SHSM) in Manufacturing, including sector-focused learning, certifications, experiential learning, career exploration, reach-ahead experiences, and sector-partnered experiences.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
Before teaching at Port Credit, I worked at Palantir, ran a startup called PetroPredict, and completed internships at Facebook, Suncor, and several smaller technology companies. Earlier, while I was still in high school, I worked as a lifeguard and deck supervisor with the City of Mississauga and in a machine shop after a co-op placement.
Outside work and school, I was a sponsored kiteboarder for Switch Kites and have been an avid box lacrosse player. Kiteboarding was a major part of my life and shaped how I think about practice, judgement, risk, feedback, equipment, weather, failure, and learning from people who have different skills, knowledge, and wisdom from you.



After moving back to Mississauga following time living abroad, kiteboarding became something I could realistically do only a few times a year. I needed other ways to keep learning with people, contributing to communities, and doing things that require practice.
I now volunteer, guest speak, and run workshops with a variety of organizations, but I spend the most time contributing to my local parish in Mississauga. I am of Goan Catholic heritage, and I have helped with children’s programs including First Holy Communion and with liturgy involving exceptional individuals.
I take my own beliefs seriously while also trying to study other philosophies and religious traditions with respect. That helps me understand more of the people I teach and work with, and gives me more ways to think about learning, discipline, community, service, attention, and human well-being. More recently, I have been training in Gong Fu and Qigong with the Chung Wah Kung Fu International System and the Human Wellness and Recuperation Centre.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
The goal is simple: useful teaching and learning material is open-source, free to access, and easy to adapt. Learners, educators, and anyone else who can use it can access basic knowledge without a paywall or dependence on a single classroom, platform, or account.
This approach is influenced by open education projects such as Tony R. Kuphaldt’s Socratic Electronics, which emphasizes learning through questions, research, discussion, explaining ideas to others, and developing the ability to teach yourself.
The material here is meant to be used, questioned, adapted, improved, and shared again.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
Many religions and philosophies contain ideas that can sound similar, much as versions of the Golden Rule appear across different traditions. Similarity does not make them identical. I do not want to flatten distinct histories, beliefs, languages, or practices into one system. These are short ideas I find useful to keep nearby when thinking about teaching, learning, practice, and community.

The Way: I use the Way here in a broad, non-doctrinal sense: being present with things as they are, without judgement, and letting the path become clearer through practice. The focus is on being rather than constantly reaching for the next outcome: doing one thing mindfully, acting effectively, accepting what is present, and working without attachment to a particular result. This also connects to well-being as something lived and practised across the physical, mental, spiritual, and emotional parts of a person. Different traditions use the idea of a way or path differently, and those differences matter.
Spirit: Spirit can describe something carried within a person, but also something strengthened between people: school spirit, team spirit, community spirit. It can grow through belonging, responsibility, shared effort, service, and the feeling that your work is connected to something larger than yourself.
Paul Cormier / Indigenous learning methodology: Kinoo’amaadawaad Megwaa Doodamawaad, translated by Cormier as “they are learning with each other while they are doing.” I want that idea to shape these notes: students learn with one another while doing real work, and the documentation grows from that work.
Confucianism: learn something, then practise it. Learning is not complete when something has merely been heard or read.
Daoism: a long journey begins beneath your feet. Large work starts from what is small and present, and care at the end matters as much as enthusiasm at the beginning.
Stoicism: Epictetus treats education as more than book knowledge; character and judgement are developed through repeated practice and self-correction.
Epicureanism: Epicurus places unusual weight on friendship as part of a good life. Learning is easier to sustain when people enjoy doing worthwhile things together.
Hindu tradition: the Bhagavad Gita 2:47 distinguishes action from attachment to its results: do the work carefully without letting the outcome become the only reason for doing it.
Buddhism: the Dhammapada 76 compares a wise person who points out your faults to someone revealing hidden treasure. Good correction can be a gift.
Jewish tradition: Pirkei Avot 4:1 asks, “Who is wise?” and answers: the person who learns from every person.
Christian tradition: “Iron sharpens iron” is a useful image for people improving one another through honest contact, practice, challenge, and care.
Islamic learning tradition: “Seek knowledge from the cradle to the grave” is a widely repeated educational maxim. It is worth carrying for its meaning, while being careful not to present it as a verified Prophetic hadith. The Qur’an also gives the concise prayer, “My Lord, increase me in knowledge”.
Ubuntu: “A person is a person through other persons.” The idea of umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu keeps learning connected to relationship, dignity, and community.
“Each one, teach one.” Knowledge becomes more useful when it moves through people instead of stopping with the first person who receives it.
OSSTF/FEESO: “Let us not take thought for our separate interests, but let us help one another.”
Port Credit: Lux numquam desit. Let light never be lacking. The light is something we keep alive for one another: showing up, sharing what we know, helping each other forward, and carrying the Way on.

The common thread is not that these traditions are identical. It is that many very different traditions take practice, humility, relationship, disciplined attention, service, and lifelong learning seriously.
The religious, spiritual, philosophical, and cultural references above describe ideas I study and influences I find useful. They are not belief requirements for students. Students are not expected to adopt, reject, defend, or disclose a religious, spiritual, Indigenous, philosophical, or non-religious belief. Classroom reflection can remain secular and can use interests, projects, community, culture, technical work, or another non-sensitive point of reference. Agreement with a belief is never assessed.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
This site is partly an attempt to continue a tradition I benefited from long before I became a teacher: educators making useful material available to people they may never meet.
Michael Franzen maintained a site that was extremely useful to me during teachers college. That site is now offline, but the example stayed with me: a teacher could put useful technical material on the open web and someone outside their classroom could learn from it.
Peter Beens has likewise shared a substantial body of educational and technical material through peter.beens.ca, beens.org, and Beens Consulting.
I also owe a great deal to the technology team at Westdale Secondary School, who shared an enormous amount of material, experience, and practical advice:

Taylor Wilson: computer and transportation technology
Dave Kipp: construction and woodworking
David Christie: mathematics, science, and general technology
Craig Ramsden: construction and woodworking
Rejean Royer: transportation technology
Principal Brian Goodram

The wooden MR. ANDRADE name tag shown in this project was made and gifted to me by teachers at Westdale. Rejean also shared with me parts of his Indigenous heritage and his practice of smudging as part of his daily life. I am grateful for the trust involved in sharing both technical knowledge and personal tradition.
This project is meant to carry that spirit forward: take what is useful, credit the people who helped, improve it where you can, and leave something behind for the next person.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
Technological Education Resources is built for teaching at Port Credit Secondary School, and its visual identity deliberately connects to the school without trying to replace the school’s own identity.
Port Credit’s secondary-school history reaches back to 1919, when a continuation school opened in the community. The PCSS Alumni Association preserves school history, yearbooks, memorabilia, and stories while supporting scholarships and selected school projects.
The Regional SciTech Program launched in September 2005. Alumni material describes it as an integrated science and technology program intended for both inquiry-oriented academic learners and hands-on learners interested in college, apprenticeships, skilled trades, and industry.
The school motto, Lux numquam desit, is a natural fit for a visual system built around the Port Credit lighthouse, learning, and the idea of carrying useful knowledge forward.
Technological Education Resources also recognizes the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation and the Indigenous history and continuing stewardship connected to this place. Purple and orange are included in the working palette as community and reflection accents that can be used thoughtfully in Indigenous learning and reconciliation contexts. They are project colours, not presented as official colours of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation.

A device that converts analog input signals to digital output.



A device that converts analog input signals to digital output. [1, p. 1211]

Absolute path



An absolute path identifies a resource from a complete root location.



An absolute path identifies a resource from a complete root location. [12]

The ratio of AC collector current, ic, to AC base current, ib



The ratio of AC collector current, ic, to AC base current, ib [1, p. 1211]

AC effective resistance



Also called: Re


The resistance of a coil for higher-frequency alternating current.



The resistance of a coil for higher-frequency alternating current. The value of Re is more than the DC resistance of the coil because it includes the losses associated with high-frequency alternating current in a coil. These losses include skin effect, eddy currents, and hysteresis losses. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





AC equivalent circuit



A circuit as it appears to an AC signal.



A circuit as it appears to an AC signal. In an AC equivalent circuit all capacitors and voltage sources appear as shorts. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





AC load line



A graph that shows all the possible values of IC and VCE when a transistor amplifier is driven by an AC signal.



A graph that shows all the possible values of IC and VCE when a transistor amplifier is driven by an AC signal. [1, p. 1211]

AC load power



Also called: PL


The AC power that is dissipated by the load, RL.



The AC power that is dissipated by the load, RL. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





AC resistance of a diode



The equivalent resistance of a forward-biased diode as it appears to small AC signals.



The equivalent resistance of a forward-biased diode as it appears to small AC signals. For a standard diode For the emitter diode in Id IE [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Acceleration



Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time and is a vector.



Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time. It is a vector, so a change in speed, direction, or both is acceleration. In calculus, acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time. Because velocity is the derivative of position or displacement with respect to time, acceleration is the second derivative of position or displacement with respect to time. Common units include metres per second squared (m/s²) and feet per second squared (ft/s²).



Category: Measurement & Motion

Accuracy is the fraction of all predictions that a classification model gets correct.

One that can control voltage or current.



One that can control voltage or current. Examples are transistors and diodes. [1, p. 1211]

Active filter



A filter that uses components or devices that have the ability to amplify such as transistors and op amps.



A filter that uses components or devices that have the ability to amplify such as transistors and op amps. [1, p. 1211]

Active region



The region of operation where the collector of a transistor acts like a current source.



The region of operation where the collector of a transistor acts like a current source. [1, p. 1211]

Active-low Logic



An active-low signal performs its named action when the signal is at logic low.



An active-low signal performs its named action when the signal is at logic low.

Additive manufacturing makes an object by joining material from digital model data, usually layer by layer. [18]

One that uses alkaline electrolyte.



One that uses alkaline electrolyte. [1, p. 1211]

Alternating Current



Also called: AC


Alternating current changes direction periodically and usually changes magnitude with time.



Alternating current changes direction periodically and usually changes magnitude with time.

All About Circuits Textbook







Alternation



One-half cycle of revolution of a conductor loop rotating through a magnetic field.



One-half cycle of revolution of a conductor loop rotating through a magnetic field. This corresponds to one-half cycle of alternating voltage or current. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Alternator



AC generator.



AC generator. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Amp-clamp probe



A meter that can measure AC currents, generally from the 60-Hz AC power line, without breaking open the circuit.



A meter that can measure AC currents, generally from the 60-Hz AC power line, without breaking open the circuit. The probe of the meter is actually a clamp that fits around the current-carrying conductor. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Ampere



Also called: A, amp, amps


The ampere (A) is the SI unit of electric current.



The ampere, symbol A, is the SI unit used to measure electric current. In basic circuit work, current values are stated in amperes or amps.



Category: Units & Notation

Current

) The SI unit of field intensity, H.

Category: Electrical & Electronics





Ampere-hour (A·h) rating



A common rating for batteries that indicates how much load current a battery can supply over a specified discharge time.



A common rating for batteries that indicates how much load current a battery can supply over a specified discharge time. For example, a battery with a 100-A.h rating can deliver 1 A for 100 h or 2 A [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Ampere-turn



Also called: A·t


Unit of magnetizing force equal to 1 A × 1 turn.



Unit of magnetizing force equal to 1 A × 1 turn. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Amplifier



An amplifier uses energy from a source to produce an output signal that follows an input with increased voltage, current, or power.



An amplifier uses energy from a source to produce an output signal that follows an input with increased voltage, current, or power.



Category: Electrical & Electronics



References



All About Circuits Textbook







Analog Input



Also called: Analogue Input


An analog input converts a voltage within an allowed range into a numerical reading.



An analog input converts a voltage within an allowed range into a numerical reading.



Category: Electrical & Electronics



References



Arduino Built-in Examples







Analog multimeter



A test instrument that is used to make voltage, current, and resistance measurements.



A test instrument that is used to make voltage, current, and resistance measurements. An analog multimeter uses a moving pointer and a printed scale to display the value of the measured quantity. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





AND Gate



An AND gate outputs 1 only when every input is 1.



An AND gate outputs 1 only when every input is 1.



Category: Electrical & Electronics



References



All About Circuits Textbook

Animation creates the appearance of change or motion by presenting a sequence of images or states over time.



Animation creates the appearance of change or motion by presenting a sequence of images or states over time. Pencil2D is used in this curriculum for introductory frame-based 2D animation. [10]



Category: Digital Design & Media

Frame

Antiresonance



A term to describe the condition of unity power factor in a parallel LC circuit.



A term to describe the condition of unity power factor in a parallel LC circuit. Antiresonance is used to distinguish it from the case of equal XL and XC values in a series LC circuit. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Apparent power



The product of voltage and current VA when V and I are out of phase.



The product of voltage and current VA when V and I are out of phase. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Arctangent



Also called: arctan


An inverse trigonometric function that specifies the angle, u, corresponding to a given tangent (tan) value.



An inverse trigonometric function that specifies the angle, u, corresponding to a given tangent (tan) value. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Armature



The part of a generator in which the voltage is produced.



The part of a generator in which the voltage is produced. In a motor, it is commonly the rotating member. Also, the movable part of a relay. [1, p. 1211]

Array



An array stores an ordered collection of values that are accessed by position or index.



An array stores an ordered collection of values that are accessed by position or index.

References



All About Circuits Textbook







Asymmetrical JFET



A JFET that has its gate regions offset from the center of the channel.



A JFET that has its gate regions offset from the center of the channel. With an asymmetrical JFET the drain and source leads cannot be interchanged. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Atom



The smallest particle of an element that still has the same characteristics as the element.



The smallest particle of an element that still has the same characteristics as the element. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Atomic number



The number of protons, balanced by an equal number of electrons, in an atom.



The number of protons, balanced by an equal number of electrons, in an atom. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics

Attention lets a neural network assign different weights to information when producing a representation or prediction.

Autotransformer



A single, tapped winding used to step up or step down voltage.



A single, tapped winding used to step up or step down voltage. [1, p. 1211]

Avalanche



The effect that causes a sharp increase in reverse current, IR, when the reverse-bias voltage across a diode becomes excessive.



The effect that causes a sharp increase in reverse current, IR, when the reverse-bias voltage across a diode becomes excessive. [1, p. 1211]

Balanced bridge



A circuit consisting of two series strings in parallel.



A circuit consisting of two series strings in parallel. The balanced condition occurs when the voltage ratio in each series string is identical. The output from the bridge is taken between the centers of each series string. When the voltage ratios in each series string are identical, the output voltage is zero and the bridge circuit is said to be balanced. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Band-pass filter



Filter that allows coupling a band of frequencies to the load.



Filter that allows coupling a band of frequencies to the load. [1, p. 1211]

Band-stop filter



Filter that prevents a band of frequencies from being coupled to the load.



Filter that prevents a band of frequencies from being coupled to the load. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Bandwidth



A range of frequencies that has a resonant effect in LC circuits.



A range of frequencies that has a resonant effect in LC circuits. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Bank



Components connected in parallel.



Components connected in parallel. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Banks in series



Parallel resistor banks that are connected in series with each other.



Parallel resistor banks that are connected in series with each other. [1, p. 1211]

Barrier potential



Also called: VB


The potential difference at the p-n junction of a diode.



The potential difference at the p-n junction of a diode. VB exists between the wall of positive and negative ions that are created as a result of free electrons diffusing from the n-side of the diode to the p-side. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Base



A thin and very lightly doped region in a transistor.



A thin and very lightly doped region in a transistor. The base is sandwiched between the emitter and collector regions. [1, p. 1211]



Category: Electrical & Electronics

A baseline model is a simple reference result used to judge whether a more complex model adds useful performance.



A baseline model is a simple reference result used to judge whether a more complex model adds useful performance.

Group of cells connected in series or parallel. [1, p. 1211]

Ubuntu Server Documentation







Bipolar Junction Transistor



Also called: BJT


A bipolar junction transistor is a three-terminal semiconductor device in which base current controls a larger collector current.



A bipolar junction transistor is a three-terminal semiconductor device in which base current controls a larger collector current.

All About Circuits Textbook

Steady current from a source used to stabilize output voltage with changes in load current.



Steady current from a source used to stabilize output voltage with changes in load current. [1, p. 1211]

Breakdown region



The region of transistor operation where a large undesired collector current flows as a result of the collector-base diode breaking down due to excessive reverse-bias voltage.



The region of transistor operation where a large undesired collector current flows as a result of the collector-base diode breaking down due to excessive reverse-bias voltage. [1, p. 1211]

Breakdown voltage



Also called: VBR


The reverse-bias voltage at which the avalanche effect occurs.



The reverse-bias voltage at which the avalanche effect occurs. The avalanche effect causes the reverse current, IR, to increase sharply. [1, p. 1212]

A bridge is printed material that spans between supported regions without support directly underneath. [20]

In a motor or generator, devices that provide stationary connections to the rotor. [1, p. 1212]

The build plate is the printer surface on which a 3D print is formed. [20]

Print orientation


3D printing







Bulk resistance



Also called: rB


The resistance of the p and n materials in a diode.



The resistance of the p and n materials in a diode. [1, p. 1212]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Burr



A burr is an unwanted raised edge or small piece of material left by a manufacturing process.



A burr is an unwanted raised edge or small piece of material left by a manufacturing process. [23]

Bypass capacitor



One that has very low reactance in a parallel path.



One that has very low reactance in a parallel path. [1, p. 1212]

Amount of heat energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 18C.



Amount of heat energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 18C. [1, p. 1212]

Capacitance



The ability to store electric charge.



The ability to store electric charge. [1, p. 1212]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Capacitive reactance



Also called: XC


A measure of a capacitor’s opposition to the flow of alternating current.



A measure of a capacitor’s opposition to the flow of alternating current. XC is measured in 2 fC XC 5 1 IC. XC applies only to sine-wave AC circuits. [1, p. 1212]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Capacitive voltage divider



A voltage divider that consists of series-connected capacitors.



A voltage divider that consists of series-connected capacitors. The amount of voltage across each capacitor is inversely proportional to its capacitance value. [1, p. 1212]



Category: Electrical & Electronics

A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between conductors separated by an insulator.



A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between conductors separated by an insulator.

Carbon-composition resistors



Resistors made of finely divided carbon or graphite mixed with a powdered insulating material.



Resistors made of finely divided carbon or graphite mixed with a powdered insulating material. [1, p. 1212]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Carbon-film resistors



Resistors made by depositing a thin layer of carbon on an insulated substrate.



Resistors made by depositing a thin layer of carbon on an insulated substrate. The carbon film is cut in the form of a spiral. [1, p. 1212]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Celsius scale



Also called: 8C


Temperature scale that uses 0° for the freezing point of water and 100° for the boiling point.



Temperature scale that uses 0° for the freezing point of water and 100° for the boiling point. Formerly called centigrade. [1, p. 1212]

Centimeter-gram-second system of units. [1, p. 1212]

A chamfer replaces a sharp edge with a flat angled face. [14]

Channel



The area or conducting region between the drain and source terminals of an FET.



The area or conducting region between the drain and source terminals of an FET. The channel can be made of either n-type or p-type semiconductor material. [1, p. 1212]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Charging




The effect of increasing the amount of charge stored in a capacitor.




The effect of increasing the amount of charge stored in a capacitor. The accumulation of stored charge results in a buildup of voltage across the capacitor. (2) The process of reversing the current, and thus the chemical action, in a cell or battery to re-form the electrodes. [1, p. 1212]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Charging current



The current that flows to and from the plates of a capacitor as the charge stored by the dielectric increases.



The current that flows to and from the plates of a capacitor as the charge stored by the dielectric increases. [1, p. 1212]



Category: Electrical & Electronics





Chassis ground



Common return for all electronic circuits mounted on one metal chassis or PC board.



Common return for all electronic circuits mounted on one metal chassis or PC board. Usually connects to one side of DC supply voltage. [1, p. 1212]

Chip capacitor



A surface-mounted capacitor.



A surface-mounted capacitor. [1, p. 1212]

Choke

Inductance with high XL compared with the R of the circuit. [1, p. 1212]

A path for current flow.



A path for current flow. [1, p. 1212]

A circuit breaker opens a circuit when current exceeds a safe condition and can normally be reset.

Circuit Schematic

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
text:
FROM THE ARCHIVE
Originally published on andrewandrade.ca. This version is included in Lore because it captures the kind of learning record this section is meant to preserve: teaching, history, identity, community, and the things carried forward.
View the source history on GitHub
It’s been years since I last wrote here. I started this blog back in fourth-year engineering while job hunting, before I joined Palantir, before robotics labs and late-night debugging sessions, before teaching, before all the twists that came after.
This week, Remembrance Day brought me back.
I had the honour of playing trumpet with our school band, not the Last Post; I’m still working to be good enough for that, but enough to stand with the group in something meaningful. Instruments in hand, everything paused for a moment, and it pulled me right back to my time in army cadets.
Even now, that first year is burned into my memory: awkward uniform, barely any badges, trying to figure out what leadership meant. Luckily we had mentors to guide us.
Cadets taught me that rank wasn’t the patch; it was the work behind it.
As we approached Remembrance Day this year, I found myself thinking about the small rituals that shaped me. Raising the flag was one of them.
Sometimes it was early, cold, or rushed, but it mattered. And I wasn’t alone.
Music also became part of those mornings, including our national anthem.
Fast-forward to high school robotics, coding, and engineering, different worlds entirely, but the same threads of discipline and responsibility ran through them.
I didn’t stay long enough in cadets to stack up badges like the mentors I admired, but the two years I spent there were full. Varied, intense, and formative, but I still loved computers.
This year, as part of preparing for our ceremony, I learned more than I expected, thanks entirely to the Student Activity Council, who did all the research.
That’s where I discovered the story of George Cardozo, one of the “Port Credit Boys.”

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
section: The Bugler They Didn’t Let Become an Officer
text:
The Bugler They Didn’t Let Become an Officer
George’s story starts decades before mine, but strangely close to home.
He was a Jamaican-born teacher, educated in Port-au-Prince and Kingston, who came to Canada and enlisted with the 4th Battalion, Canadian Expeditionary Force, on 22 September 1914.
One of the first recruits at Valcartier.



George standing


His attestation paper recorded only the essentials: his trade or calling, his date of birth, and his place of birth. Beyond those brief entries, the rest of George’s life, identity, and service must be reconstructed through the surviving evidence gathered from archival and family research.
A fuller picture, his experiences as a Jamaican-born bugler, his movement through the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and the context surrounding his enlistment, comes from the sources compiled in the project’s research. These include My Jamaican Family’s biography They Shall Grow Not Old: George Cardozo, a Casualty of …, the Canadian Virtual War Memorial entry for George Cordozo from Veterans Affairs Canada, and his digitized service file in Library and Archives Canada’s Personnel Records of the First World War.
Together, these sources allow us to understand George far more deeply than the minimal information captured on the photo.



George’s attestation paper


According to Dorothy Kew from the My Jamaican Family Blog, he was:

Five foot five
Dark complexion
“Coloured”
Roman Catholic
Teacher

With his education and background, he should have been an officer.
But because of his colour, he wasn’t given that chance.
Instead, they made him a bugler.



George sitting


Today, the role is ceremonial.
Back then, buglers woke before everyone else, played Reveille in the cold, roused officers, and handled the morning chores no one else wanted.
George still trained hard, at Ravina Barracks, on the SS Tyrolia to England, and finally to the Western Front.



Port Credit Boys


He died sometime between April 22 and 26, 1915, during the Second Battle of Ypres, the first time poison gas was used in the Great War. His body was never found.
His name is carved on the Menin Gate Memorial in Belgium with over 55,000 others who have no known grave.



Memorial


Every evening at 8 p.m., beneath his name, they still sound the Last Post.

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
section: Bugles, Flags, and the Things We Carry Forward
text:
Bugles, Flags, and the Things We Carry Forward
This year I raised my trumpet high,
Not for the Last Post’s mournful cry,
But with a deeper, steadier sight
Of all the threads that shaped my flight.
I thought of flags I used to raise,
The badges missed in younger days,
The mentors’ paths I didn’t tread,
And those who served and marched instead.
I thought of George, so much like me,
A teacher-learner meant to be,
Who left to fight through smoke and flame
And never made it home again.

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
text:
We Remember

“They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old…”
- For the Fallen, Lawrence Binyon

This post is both a return and a reminder, of the past we inherit, the stories we uncover, and the unexpected ways they shape our present.
This Remembrance Day, I played the trumpet for our school.
But I also played it for George.
And I’m honoured to remember him here.

title: Necessities & Nice-to-Haves
text: I can separate what must be true from what would simply make the design better.

title: Necessities & Nice-to-Haves
text:
Sort the criteria

Requirement: something the solution should accomplish.
Restriction: a limit the design must work within.
Necessity: a requirement or restriction that must be satisfied. Score it 10/10.
Nice-to-have: a useful improvement that is not required. Score it 1-9/10.

A necessity is not just something you strongly prefer. If it is missing, the design fails or cannot be used safely and appropriately.

title: Necessities & Nice-to-Haves
text:
Quick test
For each criterion, ask: Would the design still work without this? If yes, it is probably a nice-to-have.
Sort the criteria in the N.I.C.E. Needs Worksheet.

title: Situation & Opportunity
text:
Break down the situation

Fact: something observed, measured, or supported by evidence.
Assumption: something that may be true but still needs to be checked.
Interpretation: the meaning or explanation attached to the facts.

Example: “Three students asked where the tools go” is a fact. “Everyone finds the storage confusing” is an assumption. “The labels are the problem” is an interpretation.

title: Situation & Opportunity
text:

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
Why this is useful
Most hand-drawn logos have more than one part. A separate graphics layer for each part makes the logo easier to fix, colour, move, and animate.
An SVG can also guide a laser cutter, embroidery machine, vinyl cutter, or other machine. Clean paths and clear names make the file easier to use later.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
What you will make
You will rebuild a small landscape logo. The two mountain peaks also look like the letters AA. The finished SVG has four separate parts:

SUN
LEFT-A
RIGHT-A
RIVER



Your browser cannot play this video. Use the screenshots and steps below. 
Open the lesson video in a new tab.






NoteLevel 3 example



This is a simple Level 3 example, below 75%. It shows the required tracing and layer skills, but it is not a highly styled final design.
After the trace works, improve the shapes, spacing, colours, and style. Make your own logo look more polished and original.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
1. Fade and lock the sketch

Open the sketch in Photopea.
Rename the image layer REFERENCE.
Lower its Opacity to about 30%.
Lock the layer.

The sketch should be light enough that new black shapes are easy to see.



A faded landscape sketch on Photopea’s transparent canvas with the reference layer visible in the Layers panel.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
2. Make the sun

Choose the Ellipse Tool.
Set the tool to Shape mode.
Use a solid black fill and set the stroke to None.
Drag a circle over the sun.
Rename the new layer SUN.

Hold Shift while dragging if you want a perfect circle.



A black vector circle placed over the faded sun with a separate SUN layer in the Layers panel.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
3. Make two mountain shapes
The two peaks are separate pieces. Do not trace the whole mountain as one shape.

Choose the Pen Tool.
Choose Shape in the top bar.
Click anchor points at the bottom-left corner, the top of the first peak, and the centre valley.
Click the first anchor point again to make a closed path.
Rename the layer LEFT-A.
Start a new shape layer.
Trace the second peak and rename it RIGHT-A.

Use only a few points. Fewer points make a cleaner shape.



Two black triangular mountain shapes over the faded sketch with separate LEFT-A and RIGHT-A layers.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
4. Make the river
The river is a thin closed shape, not a brush line.

Start another new shape layer.
Click several points along the top edge of the river.
Click back along the bottom edge.
Close the path by clicking the first point.
Rename the layer RIVER.

For a smoother river, drag while placing an anchor point to make a Bézier curve. A few well-placed anchor points usually look smoother than many small ones.
Keep the shape simple. The curve does not need many points.



A thin black river shape traced below the two mountain shapes with the RIVER layer selected.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
section: 5. Hide the sketch and check the shapes
text:
5. Hide the sketch and check the shapes
Click the eye beside REFERENCE to hide the sketch.
Check the logo in black before adding colour. Black makes uneven shapes, gaps, and unwanted overlaps easier to see.



The black sun, two mountain peaks, and river on a transparent background with five clearly named layers.



Check your layers
The Layers panel should show:

RIVER
RIGHT-A
LEFT-A
SUN
REFERENCE, hidden and locked

These names become useful labels inside the SVG. In the next assignment, you can animate the sun, each peak, and the river separately.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
7. Add colour at the end

Double-click the shape thumbnail beside SUN.
Choose a colour and select OK.
Repeat for LEFT-A, RIGHT-A, and RIVER.
Use a small set of colours that are easy to tell apart.

Colour comes last because the black version makes shape problems easier to find.



The finished logo with a gold sun, two green mountain peaks, and a blue river on a transparent background.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
8. Save the editable PSD
Choose File > Save More > Save PSD/PSB. Keep PSD selected. Name the file studentnumber-lastname-layered-logo.psd, then choose Save.
The Photoshop Document (PSD) keeps the reference and all four editable shape layers.



Photopea’s Save PSD or PSB window over the finished coloured logo.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
9. Export the SVG

Keep REFERENCE hidden.
Choose File > Export as > SVG.
Name the file studentnumber-lastname-layered-logo.svg.
Leave add raster graphics off.
Leave add hidden layers off.
Choose Save.

The empty background keeps its transparency, so the SVG does not gain a white rectangle.



Photopea’s SVG export window with raster graphics and hidden layers turned off.


Open the finished four-part SVG to compare it with your file.

Every filename must begin with your student number, followed by your last name. Replace studentnumber and lastname with your own information. Example: 123456789-Smith-layered-logo.psd.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
Common issues

Everything is on one layer: undo the last shape, make a new layer, and draw that part again.
The Pen Tool makes a line instead of a filled shape: choose Shape mode before you click points.
The shape has too many bumps: remove points. Use only the points needed to show the main form.
The sketch appears in the SVG: hide REFERENCE and export again with add raster graphics and add hidden layers off.
The parts cannot move separately: check that every part is on its own shape layer.
The colours look busy: use fewer colours and keep enough contrast between nearby parts.


Design curriculum: Builds vector drawing, layer organization, revision, SVG export, and animation preparation.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
text:
By the end of this lesson:

I can tell the difference between a raster image and a vector image.
I can zoom in and find pixels in a PNG and paths in an SVG.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
text:
Why this is useful
The wrong file can look blurry or behave badly in another program. Knowing how the file works helps you choose the right image for a screen, an engraving, or a cut line. It also helps you send clear instructions to tools such as a laser cutter, vinyl cutter, embroidery machine, or CNC router.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
section: Two ways to describe an image
text:
Two ways to describe an image
A raster image is made from a grid of tiny squares called pixels. Raster images work well for photos, painted textures, and shading. A raster image can look blocky when it is made too large.
Each pixel stores one small piece of the image.
A vector image is made from shapes and paths. Its points, curves, fills, and lines can be edited. It stays sharp when it is made larger or smaller. Vector files are useful for logos, diagrams, score lines, and cut lines.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
text:
Same logo, two different files
At normal size, the PNG and SVG versions of this logo look almost the same. The difference becomes clear when you zoom in.



PNG: a grid of pixels



The PNG stores the logo as a grid of coloured squares. Those squares are called pixels.



When the PNG is enlarged, the square pixels make a stair-step edge.





SVG: shapes and paths



The SVG stores the logo as shapes and paths. The small points on a path are called nodes. Move a node to change the shape.



When the SVG is enlarged, the edge stays smooth. The blue line shows the path and the squares show editable nodes.











TipTry it



Open the PNG and SVG in your design program. Zoom in as far as you can. Look for square pixels in the PNG. Select the SVG with a path-selection tool and look for nodes.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
text:
What a machine sees
A machine path is the route that a tool follows. A laser, blade, pen, needle, or router can use vector geometry to plan that route.








File
What it stores
A good use




PNG
A grid of pixels
Photos, shading, websites, and laser engraving


SVG
Shapes, paths, and nodes
Laser cutting or scoring, vinyl cutting, pen plotting, and CNC paths



An embroidery design can begin with an SVG because its clean shapes are easy to trace and size. Embroidery software must then turn those shapes into stitches and save a machine file such as DST or PES. The embroidery machine follows the stitch file, not usually the SVG itself.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
text:
Sort by intended operation

Raster image: use when engraved tone or photographic detail is intentional.
Filled vector shape: useful for clean engraved artwork.
Open or closed vector path: useful for scoring or cutting when the machine workflow recognizes it.

Make the same symbol in three forms: a low-quality raster image, a filled vector shape, and an outline path. Make each one larger. Check the edges. Decide how a laser program may read each one.

Design curriculum: Complete this lesson after designing your own name + logo name tag. It supports TGJ2O, TDJ2O, and TIJ1O work with images, file types, design communication, and digital making.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
text:
Summary
PNG images are made from pixels. They work well for photos, shading, and screens, but their edges can become blocky when enlarged. SVG images are made from editable shapes and paths, so they stay sharp. Fabrication software can turn those paths into routes for cutting, scoring, plotting, routing, or creating embroidery stitches.

title: 2D Animation with Pencil2D | Frames, Timing & Short Loops
text:
Why this is useful
Animation helps you show change, movement, and ideas over time. The same planning skills are useful in videos, games, websites, presentations, and product demos.

title: 2D Animation with Pencil2D | Frames, Timing & Short Loops
text:
Motion is designed over time
Animation is a group of images shown in order. A frame is one image. A keyframe shows an important pose or change. The timeline controls the order and timing. Onion skinning shows nearby frames lightly so you can compare them.
Each frame shows one moment in the motion.

title: 2D Animation with Pencil2D | Frames, Timing & Short Loops
2D Animation with Pencil2D | Frames, Timing & Short Loops
text:
Classroom task: identity in motion
Animate the student’s original logo, lettermark or one simple object for 2–4 seconds. The loop should communicate one idea through timing and shape change: assemble, reveal, bounce, rotate, transform or respond. Avoid tracing a commercial mark or downloading a finished character as the answer.

title: 2D Animation with Pencil2D | Frames, Timing & Short Loops
text:
Evaluate the loop
Ask another person what they notice first. Check the timing, sudden jumps, the first and last frames, the crop, and the background. Save the editable Pencil2D file and the exported animation.
Use Blender when the goal becomes artistic 3D animation or rendering. Use parametric CAD when the goal is a dimension-driven fabrication part; those modules are planned for a later release.

Design curriculum: Complete this lesson after Raster, Vector, and SVG. It supports TGJ2O, TIJ1O, and TDJ work with planning, images, feedback, and revision.
