After completing the core engraving project, choose whether to make the plaque stand independently using feet, legs, a slot base, an easel or another support. This is not required for the first TAS name tag.
Open the Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Investigate alternatives
Do not give every student one finished stand file. Compare triangular legs, straight or angled legs, curved legs, T-feet, cross-feet, slot bases, easel backs, and two-leg systems. Ask what each solution changes about the footprint, material use, assembly, viewing angle, and centre of gravity.
The project-components library provides starting geometry for investigation. Students remain responsible for adapting dimensions, selecting a concept, testing it, and documenting why it works.
Use the focused standing-name-tag component set to compare a triangle leg, T-foot, cross-foot and easel back. Copy a concept into a new file; do not submit the palette sheet as the project. Complete the fabrication planning worksheet and follow Paper to Inkscape.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Easel reference set
The external FreePatternsArea easel set shows four variations on the same structural idea. Each uses a wide A-shaped front frame, one or more crosspieces, and a rear leg or kickstand. The variations change the ledge, hinge pieces, rear-leg adjustment and decorative openings rather than changing the basic load path.
The source describes a 5.51 in high, 3.70 in wide easel for 0.118 in material (140 × 94 mm, using 3 mm stock). It suggests scaling the complete design by \(4/3 = 1.333\) for 0.157 in (4 mm) material, which produces an easel about 7.35 in high and 4.92 in wide (187 × 125 mm). That preserves every proportion, including the slots. It is not the best method when you want to change the display height without changing the material thickness. In that case, resize the structure and reset every slot from the measured material instead.






WarningReference, not a verified cutting file



The SVG declares a numerical viewBox but does not declare a physical unit. Import it using a known reference dimension, confirm the intended 5.51 in (140 mm) assembled height, and measure every slot before cutting. The files have not been physically verified by Technology Commons.
The source currently identifies the design as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for personal, non-commercial use. Preserve the FreePatternsArea credit and check the current licence terms before using or sharing the files. These external files are not covered by the Technology Commons CC BY-SA licence.


Reference formats: SVG, DXF, DWG, CDR, PDF, and PNG preview.

How to read the flat reference files
The six downloads above are alternate formats of the same reference sheet. For the Technology Commons workflow, open the SVG in Inkscape. Use the PDF or PNG only to look at or print the design. DXF and DWG are for CAD/CAM software, and CDR is for CorelDRAW.
The outlines are flat parts, not a picture of the assembled easel. In the cropped example, the large A-shaped outline is the front frame and the large T-shaped outline is the wide single rear support. That T-shaped part is the large single leg: its wide top provides an attachment or hinge zone and its broad centre reaches the table. It does not stand by itself. The complete design still needs the front frame, an attachment between the parts, and a stop or tether that controls the opening angle.
The source sheet does not label every part or provide a verified step-by-step assembly sequence. Keep each apparent group together, prototype it in cardboard, and do not guess the purpose of an isolated small outline. For a clearer original starting point, choose Wide single easel back · like the reference in the Leg & Support Builder; the tool now shows both the flat cut part and a coloured assembled view.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
What the legs actually do



Front and side force diagrams for a three-legged A-frame easel



Two splayed front legs
The two front legs carry most of the vertical load. Their feet are farther apart than their tops, so the front support width is large without making the top bulky. The load should travel mostly along the plane of the sheet and down the legs as compression. Sheet material is much stiffer in its own plane than it is when pushed sideways out of plane.
The space between the legs is not only decorative. Removing low-demand material reduces mass while leaving a deep outer frame. The remaining rail width must still resist cracking at slots, grain defects and narrow corners.


Rear kickstand
The rear leg changes the frame from a nearly flat object into a triangle. In side view, the front feet and rear foot form a support footprint. The stand remains stable while the vertical projection of the combined centre of mass stays inside that footprint.
Moving the rear foot farther back increases the tipping margin and usually reduces the force needed to balance the display. It also creates a longer, more slender leg. A loose pivot or a sideways bump can then make the leg bend or buckle. The rear leg works best when its top pivot and bottom contact keep the main force close to the leg’s centreline, so the part carries compression instead of acting like a long cantilever.


Cross rail and ledge
The cross rail ties the two front legs together. It resists racking, where the frame changes from a symmetric A shape into a skewed shape, and splaying, where the feet move apart. The ledge carries the displayed object and transfers that load into both front legs. A ledge attached at only one small tab creates a concentrated bending force; two separated tabs or a continuous shoulder distribute the load more effectively.


Pivot, tabs and slots
The pivot carries shear between the front frame and rear leg while allowing the angle to change. A larger hole removes more of the leg’s net section, and a hole close to an edge can split the remaining material. Keep useful material around the hole, use a washer or smooth spacer where appropriate, and test repeated opening and closing.
Tabs and slots locate parts and transfer shear through bearing on their faces. The shoulder, not the fragile tip of a tab, should stop the part at its final position. Make the slot from measured thickness plus a tested fit adjustment; do not assume nominal plywood thickness is exact.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Bending force and size
The basic bending moment is:
\[M = F L\]
where \(F\) is the applied force and \(L\) is the perpendicular distance to the section being checked. Doubling the display load or doubling the lever arm doubles the bending moment.
For a long member behaving roughly like a cantilever, deflection changes approximately with:
\[\delta \propto \frac{F L^3}{E I}\]
This explains why a leg that is merely twice as long can feel about eight times more flexible when its cross-section is unchanged. \(E\) describes the material stiffness and \(I\) describes how the material is distributed around the bending axis.
For a rectangular strip bending out of the sheet plane, \(I\) includes the material thickness cubed. Increasing thickness from 0.118 in to 0.157 in (3 to 4 mm) can therefore increase weak-axis bending stiffness by roughly \((4/3)^3 = 2.37\) when the other dimension stays the same. Increasing thickness from 0.118 in to 0.236 in (3 to 6 mm) gives roughly \(2^3 = 8\) times the weak-axis stiffness. Real plywood varies by species, ply quality, grain direction, voids, moisture and cut quality, so these ratios explain trends rather than certify a load.
The most effective design move is not simply making every leg thick. Keep forces in plane, use a triangular footprint, shorten unsupported lengths, tie the front legs together, and avoid eccentric joints that twist the sheet.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Starting proportions to investigate
These are prototype starting points for a light display easel, not structural ratings:








Feature
Starting relationship
Why it matters




Front footprint width
about 0.6 to 0.75 of easel height
improves side-to-side tipping resistance


Rear-foot distance
about 0.35 to 0.5 of easel height
improves front-to-back tipping resistance


Front leg or frame-rail width
at least 4 to 6 material thicknesses
leaves a useful net section around cutouts and slots


Cross-rail depth
at least 4 material thicknesses
helps resist racking and leg splay


Tab length along an edge
at least 4 material thicknesses
distributes bearing instead of concentrating it at one small tab


Material beside a slot
at least 2 material thicknesses as a first check
reduces splitting at the slot end



For 0.118 in (3 mm) stock, those starting relationships suggest front rails around 0.47 to 0.71 in wide, a cross rail at least about 0.47 in deep, and a tab at least about 0.47 in long. These are hypotheses to test with the actual stock, not guaranteed minimums.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Worked example: 11 × 4 inch name plate
Assume the plaque is 11 inches wide, 4 inches high and nominally 1/8 inch thick. Measure the actual material rather than entering exactly 0.125 inch automatically. Define the viewing angle from the tabletop: 75 degrees is 15 degrees back from vertical, while 80 degrees is 10 degrees back from vertical.









Viewing angle
Top moves behind the bottom
Vertical rise
Centre-of-mass projection behind the bottom




75°
1.04 in
3.86 in
0.52 in


80°
0.69 in
3.94 in
0.35 in



The centre-of-mass values assume a uniform plaque without a heavy attachment. The support footprint must extend behind that projected point, with additional margin for bumps and material variation.

Stronger, quieter option: two high supports

Put two triangular cheeks or rear legs about 1.5 to 2 inches in from each end of the 11-inch plaque.
Attach each support about 3 to 3.5 inches above the bottom edge.
Start with the rear contact about 1.5 to 1.75 inches behind the plaque’s bottom contact.
A rear member from a 3.25-inch-high attachment to that footprint is about 3.2 to 3.4 inches long at the proposed angles.

The pair distributes load across the plaque and resists twisting. The higher attachment gives the support more leverage to resist rotation, but the longer member needs enough width to prevent sideways bending. A triangular cheek is usually stiffer than a narrow stick because it shortens the unsupported load path.


Sleeker option: one low centre support
A single centred support can attach about 1.25 inches above the bottom, place its rear contact about 1.25 inches behind the bottom, and use a member about 1.5 to 1.6 inches long. This is compact and visually quiet, but the smaller vertical spacing creates greater force at the joint for the same overturning moment. One central support also provides less resistance to twisting across an 11-inch-wide plaque.
Use two separated bottom locating points or a continuous ledge even if there is only one rear leg. They stop the plaque from rotating around the centre support. Widening the concealed base of the centre support also improves side-to-side stability without making the visible leg taller.


Prototype sequence

Draw both side profiles full size on half a sheet of paper or cardboard.
Test 75 degrees and 80 degrees. Choose the smallest tilt that still reads well under the expected viewing height.
Test the two-support version first as the reference design.
Remove material or move toward a single centre support only after the reference design passes the push tests.
Measure the real 1/8-inch stock and cut a slot coupon. Set the slot from measured thickness plus the tested fit adjustment.
Push at both ends and at the top centre. Watch for tipping, plaque twist, slot splitting and out-of-plane leg bending.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Stability checks

Locate the combined centre of mass approximately over the support area.
Increase the support footprint where tipping is likely.
Consider plaque height, thickness, angle, and the direction of expected bumps.
Test front-to-back and side-to-side stability.
Push lightly from both sides and watch for out-of-plane leg bending or pivot twist.
Check whether the cross rail prevents the front legs from spreading.
Check whether slots weaken a narrow region or create fragile grain directions.
Inspect the net material around every pivot hole and slot end.
Record what changed between versions.
Label the load path and the interface that locates the engraved blank.
Test the stand with the actual blank rather than a guessed rectangle.

Use cardboard or scrap material for a quick geometry prototype before cutting the full design. A stand that works only on a perfectly still surface needs another iteration.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Supports TIJ1O and TDJ2O design-process learning through alternatives, modelling, stability, constraints, testing, feedback, and iteration. Construction and manufacturing contexts may connect to TCJ2O and TMJ2O.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text: Calibration is not one magic kerf value. It is a short, recorded test that connects this sheet, this machine condition, this geometry, and this intended fit.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
Operating procedure or material calibration?



Operating procedure


Machine-specific setup, safety instruction, assessments, and authorization are not provided on this public website. Follow your school board’s safety guidelines and the course-specific instruction provided by your teacher. Students in Mr. Andrade’s classes can find that information in Google Classroom.




Material calibration


Measure how one stock-and-setting combination changes size and fit. This is about the result of the process.



Actual thickness and batch are recorded.


A known drawing dimension imports at 100%.


Cut width and finished dimensions are measured.


Slots and holes are tested against the real mating object.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
1 · Measure the actual sheet
Plywood sold as 1/4 inch may not measure 6.35 mm. Measure at several locations with callipers, including near a visibly damaged edge but not on it. Record the minimum, maximum and the value used to design the test.

Material thicknessRecord a measured range, not a catalogue assumption. Ruler / scale checkConfirm millimetres and 100% import before cutting. Dimension verificationCompare a known drawing dimension to the finished result.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
2 · Understand what kerf changes
The beam removes a narrow band centred on the path. With the path drawn on the intended boundary, an outside part tends to finish smaller and an inside opening tends to finish larger. The magnitude varies, so do not copy a universal number.



Kerf diagram showing the cut band around a vector path, a smaller outside part and a larger inside opening.


BRM’s current kerf and kerf-compensation explanation is a useful process reference. BRM also hosts a free kerf gauge SVG, credited there to Nameek and Elplatt, and explicitly tells users to check scale after import. Use it as another test method, not as a pre-approved local setting.
Ponoko’s 2011 article, Figuring out kerf for precision parts, is included only as a historical/conceptual example of test-and-revise thinking. Do not copy its old settings or service-specific assumptions.

Kerf testMeasure a repeated cut rather than guessing from one edge. Tab fitTest the male feature and its orientation. Slot fitStart from measured thickness, then compare a small series. Four-fit seriesName the function: loose, sliding, snug or press. Hole fitTest the actual bottle, dowel or fastener, not only a calliper.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
3 · Cut, measure and decide

Open one test SVG in Inkscape and confirm document units, viewBox scale and a known dimension.
Label the coupon with material, batch, date, machine and revision before cutting.
Use the course-specific process provided by your teacher.
Let the coupon cool and measure it consistently; do not force a calliper into a soft or angled edge.
Test the real mating object in every candidate feature.
Select the fit that serves the function. A press fit is not automatically “more accurate” than a sliding fit.
Update the source dimension, save the record and repeat only the smallest necessary test.







Warning



Kerf compensation changes geometry; it does not correct a machine-condition problem, warped stock, or an incorrectly scaled import. Resolve unexpected machine behaviour through the course-specific process before interpreting the coupon.

System decisions
Consider a French cleat or other approved removable mounting interface, a thicker structural backer, 1/4 inch precision faces, dowels, pins, screws, holes, slots, combs, trays, labels, and shadow-board cues. Design a handle or safe grip only if it does not interfere with mounted use or tool retention.
The wall rail, wall attachment, load path, and structural fasteners must be selected and approved for the actual installation. A thin laser-cut plywood face is not a rated wall-mounting system.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
A laser cutter makes accurate flat parts. The finished object also depends on how those parts locate one another, how loads move through the joints, how much surface is available for bonding, and how the edges and faces are finished.






ImportantScope of this lesson

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
Adhesive choices








Adhesive
Typical design use
Design consideration




Wood glue
Close-fitting wood, plywood or MDF joints
Works best when the mating surfaces fit well and provide useful bonded area. Select the exact product for the material and environment.


White glue
Paper, cardboard, light wood and general porous-material assemblies
Useful for classroom models and lighter work, but do not assume it has the same strength or moisture resistance as a purpose-selected wood glue.


Epoxy
Mixed materials, small gaps, repairs or assemblies that need a rigid bond
A two-part system can bond several material types and fill space, but the specific product determines cure, gap and finish behaviour.


Super glue (cyanoacrylate)
Small, close-fitting parts that need a quick bond
Fast setting leaves little repositioning time. Test it on the real material because appearance and bond behaviour vary.


Glue stick
A temporary adhesion or separation layer on a compatible 3D-printer build plate
This is not a structural adhesive and is not for a laser-cutter bed. Follow the printer and filament guidance for the exact build surface.



Adhesive should support a good joint, not hide a poor fit. Keep glue away from visible surfaces that will be stained because sealed patches can absorb colour differently.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
section: Joint geometry, surface area and strength
text:
Joint geometry, surface area and strength

Butt joint: simple, but it offers little alignment and may have limited bonded area.
Lap or half-lap: overlaps material to increase contact area and resist sliding.
Tab-and-slot joint: locates parts and can transfer force when the tab, slot and material thickness match.
Finger or box joint: repeats interlocking fingers to increase bonded area and create a visible pattern.
Mortise-and-tenon form: uses a projecting part and a receiving opening to locate an assembly.
Keyed, wedged or interlocking joint: uses geometry or a separate key to hold parts in position.
Layered or laminated joint: stacks cut profiles to create thickness, relief or a stronger local feature.

More bonded surface area can spread a load, but area alone does not guarantee strength. Also consider grain direction, sheet thickness, fit, leverage, notches, stress concentration, material quality and the selected adhesive.

Learn from Japanese joinery
Japanese joinery can inspire precise shoulders, keys, wedges and interlocking forms. Study how the geometry locates parts and manages force, then adapt the principle to sheet material and the project’s actual loads. A laser-cut imitation of a traditional joint is not automatically strong, so test fit and performance in the real material.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
section: Design the appearance of the joint

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
Cleanup and shaping tools







Tool
Useful for




File or needle file
Refining tabs, slots, straight edges and small openings with control.


Rasp
Removing wood quickly and shaping larger outside profiles.


Sanding block
Keeping broad faces and straight edges flat while smoothing them.


Belt sander
Faster material removal on accessible outside edges and surfaces.


Oscillating spindle sander
Smoothing inside curves, openings and concave edges.


Coping saw
Trimming notches or internal shapes before final filing and sanding.


Fine abrasive paper
Final smoothing and easing exposed corners without removing too much material.



Cleanup must preserve the dimensions that make a joint work. Keep a locating shoulder square when the assembly depends on it, while easing exposed corners when that improves touch and appearance.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
Sanding and staining wood
Sanding can remove residue, level faces, soften exposed corners and prepare a consistent surface. Do not sand away the fit of tabs, slots or calibrated edges. Move from shaping to finer finishing only as much as the material and intended appearance require.
Stain changes colour and can emphasize grain, but laser-cut edges, glue residue and different sheet layers may absorb it unevenly. Test the complete combination on an offcut: cut edge, sanded face, adhesive and stain. Decide whether the project benefits from preserving the dark cut edge, sanding it lighter, or making every edge treatment consistent.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
Assembly and finish check

Do the joints locate the parts without forcing them?
Is there enough well-fitted bonded area for the intended load?
Are high-stress notches, thin tabs or long lever arms creating a weak point?
Does the cleanup method preserve critical dimensions?
Are visible joints, grain, edges and stain part of one aesthetic decision?
Has the material, adhesive and finish combination been tested on an offcut?

title: Laser Cutting for Technology Education | SVG, Kerf, Fits & Fabrication
text:
These canonical notes support a simple first TAS project and a deeper reusable fabrication pathway. Students can learn engraving versus cutting, SVG preparation, scale, material measurement, kerf, fit, holes, slots and tabs, supports, assemblies, adhesive selection, cleanup, sanding, staining, hybrid fabrication and testing without treating every lesson as a required project.
The learning sequence lives here. The separate Laser Fabrication Library holds downloadable SVGs, calibration files, editable geometry, project components, holders, and inspiration.
For the active name-tag project, use the classroom toolkit. For advanced work, the toolkit also includes component palettes, standing-name-tag ideas, five pill-bottle organizer references and teaching slides. Set display units and document units to mm.
Set the page to the intended physical output size.
Save immediately as project-name_v01_master.svg.
Turn on snapping only when it supports the intended datum and alignment; do not let snapping replace entered dimensions.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Bring in building blocks
If the project begins as a plate with a row, grid, radial or perimeter hole pattern, use the Fabrication Plate Builder first. Its output is intentionally plain: CUT_OUTER, CUT_HOLES and an optional GUIDES group. Inkscape remains the place to add labels, slots, custom profiles and manufacturing intent.

Open the relevant component palette.
Select the named component group and copy it into the master file.
Use the toolbar or Object → Transform to enter exact width, height and position.
Rename the group by purpose: top-shelf, bottle-hole-01, left-gusset.
Duplicate repeated parts from one checked original. Use Object → Align and Distribute for centres and spacing.

Avoid advanced node editing in the first sequence. If a shape requires many uncontrolled node moves, return to simpler parts or revise the paper plan.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Separate manufacturing intent
Use clearly named groups or layers for CUT, SCORE and ENGRAVE. The library uses red, blue and black as a communication convention, but the machine operator confirms the local mapping. A colour alone is never approval to cut.
For the first name-tag engraving, set the page to the measured pre-cut blank, keep artwork inside the safe margin, hide/delete guides, and export the page as PNG at the instructor-set resolution. Reopen the PNG and confirm pixel dimensions, crop and orientation before it enters the laser workflow.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Preflight

Page width, page height and intended object size are correct in mm.
Every critical dimension matches the paper plan.
One controlled original was used for duplicates.
No duplicate paths, stray objects, hidden output or critical external fonts remain.
The machine preview contains the expected count of cuts and engraves.
A fit coupon was made for slots, holes, hardware or measured objects.
The filename shows project and version; obsolete versions are not sent accidentally.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Evidence to submit
Submit the paper plan, editable SVG master, fabrication/export file, photograph or measurement from the test, and one sentence naming what changed in the next version.
Use Material Fit + Calibration whenever a dimension must mate with real stock, hardware or an object.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
Choose an existing tool holder, organizer, fixture, or storage product as a precedent. Study what it does well, identify a real opportunity, then create an original design that improves the experience for a defined user and context.
The goal is not to make a copy. The goal is to learn from a good idea, explain how it works, and produce a better response to the problem using your own measurements, geometry, testing, and documentation.
Your evidence should justify each criterion, make every trade-off visible, and show at least one iteration.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
Choose an existing tool holder, organizer, fixture, or storage product as a precedent. Study what it does well, identify a real opportunity, then create an original design that improves the experience for a defined user and context.
The goal is not to make a copy. The goal is to learn from a good idea, explain how it works, and produce a better response to the problem using your own measurements, geometry, testing, and documentation.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
The design challenge
Develop a tool holder or organizer that improves at least three of these qualities:

Faster: quicker to fabricate, assemble, install, use, inspect, clean, or return tools to.
Cheaper: less material, fewer parts, common hardware, shorter machine time, or lower replacement cost.
Better looking: clearer proportions, stronger visual hierarchy, intentional colour and form, or a better fit with its setting.
More ergonomic: easier reach, a safer grip, better visibility, comfortable clearances, and one-hand use where appropriate.
More positive: creates calm, confidence, pride, delight, belonging, or satisfaction instead of clutter and frustration.
More useful: holds the right objects, supports a wider range, or solves a problem the precedent misses.
More durable or serviceable: stronger load path, replaceable wear parts, accessible fasteners, or easier repair.
More responsible: less waste, fewer mixed materials, efficient sheet layout, or parts that can be reused.

Every gain has a possible trade-off. A cheaper design may take longer to assemble. A smaller design may make tools harder to grasp. State what improved, what did not, and what evidence supports the claim.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
1. Find precedents
Collect at least three references from two different source types. Include one commercial product and one build, model, or assembly that reveals how parts might work together.

Product and laser-project ideas

Etsy tool-holder results: compare use cases, forms, prices, claims, and recurring themes in public reviews. Do not copy seller photos, artwork, or files.
Glowforge Catalog: study laser-cut construction, layer strategies, visual language, and product categories. Catalog access does not grant permission to redistribute or recreate a paid design.
Instructables tool-organizer search: look for build sequences, material choices, mistakes, tests, and revisions.



Mechanisms and fabrication ideas

Printables tool-holder search: inspect mounting, retention, modularity, print orientation, user makes, ratings, and comments.
Thingiverse tool-holder and organization group: compare holders for specific tools with broader workshop systems.
MakerWorld tool-holder collection: study adjustable, magnetic, modular, and low-support approaches.



Assemblies and form studies

Onshape public documents: use the Public filter to study part relationships, assemblies, parameters, and drawings.
Sketchfab tool-holder models: rotate models to inspect form, access, and assembly. Check the licence on each model before downloading or reusing anything.



Graphics and visual language

Openverse, Openclipart, and Noun Project: investigate symbols, silhouettes, and graphic styles for labels. Check the individual licence and attribution requirement before use.

Start locally too: browse the Laser Fabrication Library, purpose-built holder kits, five organizer reference assemblies, and Tool Organizer Gallery.
For more starting points, use the public libraries above and add teacher-reviewed references on inclusive design, repair, CAD, graphics, museum scans, electronics, and sustainability. A teacher must review each entry before classroom use.






ImportantPublicly visible does not mean free to copy



Record the creator or seller, page title, URL, access date, and stated licence for every reference. You may analyze publicly observable functions, interfaces, proportions, mechanisms, and user feedback. Do not trace product photographs, reproduce logos or distinctive decoration, download files without permission, bypass payment, or present another person’s work as your own. Reuse a file only when its licence clearly permits your intended use, and provide the required attribution.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
section: 2. Reverse engineer the problem, not the artwork
text:
2. Reverse engineer the problem, not the artwork
For each precedent, make an evidence table.







Question
Evidence to record




Who is it for?
User, setting, tools, reach zone, and likely routine


What problem does it solve?
Need, current frustration, and desired result


How does it work?
Support, retention, mounting, labels, load path, and assembly


What looks successful?
Features supported by photographs, specifications, build notes, or repeated review themes


What could improve?
Specific issue, affected user, and evidence rather than a guess


What cannot be confirmed online?
Hidden dimensions, material grade, strength, comfort, fit, or long-term durability



Treat reviews as clues, not facts. Look for repeated observations, separate shipping or seller issues from product-design issues, and verify what you can with direct measurement and testing.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
3. Write an improvement brief
Use this sentence frame:

Design an original [product] for [user and setting] that [solves the need]. It must [three measurable criteria] while respecting [material, machine, time, safety, and cost constraints].

Turn broad intentions into testable criteria.







Intention
Testable version




Faster
A user can identify, remove, and return the selected tool in 10 seconds or less.


Cheaper
The design fits within the assigned sheet area and uses no more than two purchased fastener types.


Better looking
Three users can identify the intended tool group and describe the visual hierarchy without prompting.


More ergonomic
The target tools can be removed with one hand without pinching neighbouring tools or twisting the wrist sharply.


More positive
User feedback includes a chosen feeling, such as calm or confidence, and identifies the feature that created it.


More serviceable
A damaged holder component can be replaced without discarding the backer or removing unrelated tools.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
4. Generate and select concepts

Measure the real tools, mounting area, stock, and critical hand clearances.
Sketch at least three meaningfully different concepts. Changing only decoration does not create a new concept.
Annotate the support method, retention method, mounting interface, assembly order, and expected load path.
Score each concept against the criteria using a decision matrix.
Explain the selected concept and one trade-off you accepted.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
section: 5. Build evidence before the full product

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
Assessment focus







Area
Evidence of strong work




Investigation
Varied, relevant, attributed precedents and careful interpretation of user evidence


Originality
New geometry and decisions tied to this user, tool set, and context


Improvement
Clear, measurable gains in at least three selected qualities


Technical quality
Accurate measurement, suitable tolerances, efficient layout, and intentional assembly


Testing
A critical question tested early with recorded results and a meaningful revision


Communication
Clear drawings, source links, licences, comparison, and honest claim language




Ontario curriculum relevance: Adaptable to TIJ1O, TDJ2O, TMJ2O, TTJ2O, TCJ2O, TEJ2O, and senior design or manufacturing courses. The teacher should select a scope, process, and assessment emphasis appropriate to the course and available equipment. Machine-specific safety information follows school board guidelines and the course information provided by the teacher; students in Mr. Andrade’s classes use Google Classroom for that material.

Continue with the Tool Organizer Gallery and design criteria, widen the investigation with the public libraries above, then use the Fabrication Planning Worksheet to document the selected direction.

title: CAD Tools
text:
Use these tools to turn measurements and construction ideas into editable geometry. Check every generated part against the real material, machine, and assembly before fabrication.


Fabrication Plate Builder
Create a measured plate with repeated holes and download a true-size SVG.


Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
Compare support styles and generate editable support geometry.


Tool Organizer Gallery
Study documented tool-holder designs, criteria, and revisions.

title: Fabrication Plate Builder
text: This browser tool makes repeatable plate geometry. It opens in inches. A millimetre toggle remains available when a machine or material specification needs it; changing the unit converts the current values instead of changing the physical size. The downloaded SVG keeps the selected physical unit. The tool does not choose safe material, machine settings, joints, mounting hardware, or a final fit.

title: Fabrication Plate Builder
text:
What the downloads contain

Cut SVG: the actual full-size plate outline and holes. Open this in Inkscape or compatible laser software. Red paths are cut geometry. Optional guides, including the A-D corner labels, are not cut paths.
Settings JSON: a text record of every builder value. It is useful for documentation or troubleshooting, but it is not a laser-cut file and this version of the builder does not import it.
Share link: the current settings stored in the web address. Send or bookmark this when you want the builder to reopen the same design.


Diameter and radius, without the jargon

For a circle, set Outer diameter. The tool calculates its radius as half the diameter.
For a ring, set Outer diameter and Ring wall thickness. The ring’s inner opening is the outer diameter minus twice the wall thickness.
For a rounded rectangle, set Width, Height, and Corner radius. Corner radius affects only the four outside corners.
For a holder hole, either measure the object and add clearance, or choose Direct finished diameter and enter the final circle size yourself.
For corner holes, Hole centre measures from each adjoining plate edge to the centre of the circle. Nearest edge of hole measures the remaining material between the circle and those straight edges. The preview labels the corners A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right) and D (bottom left).

title: Fabrication Plate Builder
text:
What happens next


1 · BuilderSet the base, measured opening, pattern and spacing. Resolve every red validation message.


2 · InkscapeOpen the SVG at 100%, confirm the document units and dimensions, then add labels, slots or project-specific geometry.


3 · Test couponUse the laser fabrication library to test the actual stock, machine and fit.


4 · OnshapeUse CAD when the design depends on 3D joints, motion, assemblies, toleranced interfaces or more than one plane.


The laser fabrication library is the idea and part library. This builder generates repeated plate geometry. Inkscape is the 2D finishing environment. Onshape is the better tool for assemblies and 3D relationships. These are complementary workflows, not interchangeable buttons.
Need supports for the plate? Open the Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder to generate straight, angled, triangular, cross-foot or rear-easel parts with measured slots.
Planning the complete holder? Use the Tool Organizer Gallery and design criteria to check visibility, labels, access, stability, wall mounting and modularity.

title: Tool Organizer Gallery
section: What makes a good tool holder?
text:
What makes a good tool holder?







Design criterion
What a student should be able to show




Visible inventory
Every tool or part has a visible position. A missing item can be noticed quickly.


Clear labels
Names, sizes, outlines or colour-independent symbols show where each item belongs.


Easy access
A user can see the handle, grip it and remove or return the tool without moving neighbouring tools.


Secure fit
The holder supports the tool without being so tight that normal removal becomes difficult. Sharp or fragile parts are protected.


Freestanding stability
The holder stands on its own and does not tip when a tool is removed from an outside position.


Wall option
The design can include a tested wall interface, such as a French cleat, while still allowing safe removal or service. Mounting hardware must suit the actual wall and load.


Stacking or modularity
Modules can align, connect or stack without hiding labels, blocking tools or becoming unstable.


Simple construction
Parts, joints and fasteners are understandable, buildable and replaceable.



Not every holder needs every feature. Choose the criteria that matter for the tools, user and location, then test those claims.

title: Tool Organizer Gallery
text:
A practical test

Glance test: Can another student identify every tool and notice what is missing?
Reach test: Can the user remove and return each tool with a natural grip?
Tip test: Does the organizer remain stable when the heaviest outside tool is removed?
Carry test: Can it be moved without loose tools falling out or the structure flexing?
Mount test: If it hangs, can it be attached, removed and loaded without pulling away, rotating or lifting off accidentally?

Record the result of each test. A claim such as “wall-mountable,” “portable” or “stable” is not complete until the actual interface has been built and tested.

title: Tool Organizer Gallery
text:
From measurements to a prototype

Compare the finished examples and decide which features fit the real tools and user.
Measure the real tools, including handles, collars, tapers and the hand clearance needed for removal.
Draw the concept using orthographic views and an isometric or assembly view.
Use the Fabrication Plate Builder for plates, rings and repeated holder holes.
Use the Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder when the organizer needs a freestanding base, legs or a rear support.
Browse the Laser-Cut Gallery for reusable geometry and design directions.
Make a small fit test before building the complete prototype.
Photograph the build, collect feedback and record the next revision.

title: Tool Organizer Gallery
text:
Add a future build
Each new organizer page should include a full finished photo, the original drawing, the problem, key dimensions, materials, fabrication method, what worked, feedback, the next revision, downloads where appropriate and a clear validation status.
Do not mark a design “validated” merely because a file renders or a digital assembly looks plausible. Distinguish drawing available, dimension-tested, fit-tested, shop-tested and photo documented. If evidence is missing, say so instead of filling the gap with a stock or generated image.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
I can use colour for emphasis without making colour the only cue.
I can measure text and graphic contrast.
I can test the final screen, print, or fabricated result and revise it.







Note



The lesson applies the BBC guidance for visually and hearing impaired audiences. WCAG 2.2 ratios are added so students have a measurable test as well as a visual comparison.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
I can use colour for emphasis without making colour the only cue.
I can measure text and graphic contrast.
I can test the final screen, print, or fabricated result and revise it.







Note



The lesson applies the BBC guidance for visually and hearing impaired audiences. WCAG 2.2 ratios are added so students have a measurable test as well as a visual comparison.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Why this is useful
“Looks different” is not a reliable contrast test. Two colours can have different hues and still be almost the same lightness. Measure the pair, then test the real output.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Use a measurable minimum


Clear contrast
12.6:1 · comfortably above the minimum


Minimum contrast
4.5:1 · passes for normal-size text


Weak contrast
2.0:1 · fails for text and essential graphics


Large text, at least 24 px regular or about 18.5 px bold, can use 3:1. Essential icons, controls, and graphic boundaries also need 3:1. Do not round: 4.49:1 does not meet 4.5:1.
These are WCAG 2.2 Level AA thresholds for digital content. They are a starting point, not a promise that every person or output device will find the result easy to use. Aim higher when you can.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Compare the guide’s examples




Black text on white and white text on black are labelled good contrast. Pale green on yellow and pale grey on light grey are labelled bad contrast.



Light-dark difference matters
The top two pairs have a large value difference. The bottom pairs do not. Source noted in the guide.






Six colour pairs place bad contrast examples in a left column and better contrast versions in a right column.



Hue is not enough
Changing the background value makes each word easier to separate, even when the hue remains similar. Source noted in the guide.






Green text on red and pale blue text on blue are labelled bad choices. Pale yellow text on dark green is labelled a good choice.



Some pairs interfere
Red-green and similar-blue pairs can fail for different reasons. The final pair adds a clear light-dark difference. Source noted in the guide.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Do not use colour alone
If colour communicates a status, category, warning, or selected state, add another cue.


Add a label
Write Pass and Revise, not just green and red dots.


Add a shape or pattern
Use different marker shapes, line styles, or fill patterns in a chart.


Add position
Keep categories in a stable order and label them directly.


Add emphasis
Use weight, size, an icon, or a border together with colour.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Test the real result

Check the design at its final size, not only while zoomed in.
Use a contrast checker for digital text and essential graphics.
View a greyscale copy.
Test on the target projector, printer, material, cutter, or engraver.
Show it without explaining it. Ask what the person noticed first and what was difficult to understand.
Revise and test again.

For fabrication, make a small sample before the final piece. Check thin lines, small gaps, inside spaces, surface finish, and lighting.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Check your work

Normal-size text meets at least 4.5:1.
Large text and essential non-text graphics meet at least 3:1.
Colour is never the only signal.
Text over a photograph has a dependable background or a tested halo.
The real output has been checked from the expected viewing distance.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Summary
Measure contrast, add a second cue, and test the actual output. Return to the Accessible Design guide and use the four checks before publishing.
Sources: W3C Understanding Contrast Minimum, W3C Understanding Non-text Contrast, and W3C Understanding Use of Color.

title: Accessible Design
text:
Graphics Accommodation Guide



Accessible design is not a separate style. It is the work of making sure the idea survives small type, colour changes, busy backgrounds, printing, projection, and fabrication.

Follow the guide





Google Docs showing the Alt text panel for a selected image.

A colour wheel shown in full colour and in greyscale. Several different hues become similar grey values.

Three panels label red with green text and blue with lighter blue text as bad choices, and green with pale yellow text as a good choice.

Significant figures
Significant figures show the precision of a measured or stated value. Keep full calculator precision and round once, at the end.
0.00420 has three significant figures.
\(6.23 \times 1.23 = 7.6629\), reported as 7.66.
For multiplication and division, use the same number of significant figures as the least precise input. For addition and subtraction, use the least precise decimal place.

title: Circuits
text:
Ohm’s law and power
Ohm’s law connects voltage, current, and resistance.
\[
V = IR \qquad I = \frac{V}{R} \qquad R = \frac{V}{I}
\tag{1}\]
Equation Equation 1 gives the three general forms of Ohm’s law.
Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer:
\[
P = VI \qquad P = I^2R \qquad P = \frac{V^2}{R}
\tag{2}\]
Use Equation Equation 2 only after identifying the known quantities.
Use volts (V), amperes (A), ohms (\(\Omega\)), and watts (W). Convert prefixes before substituting, then report the final answer with the appropriate prefix and significant figures.

title: Circuits
text:
GUESS method
Put each part on its own line.
G: Given: list each known value with its symbol and unit.
U: Unknown: list each value you must find.
E: Equation: choose a general equation.
S: Substitute: rearrange first, then substitute values with units.
S: Solve: show the unrounded result, check it, then round once.
For a Casio calculator, enter one calculation per line. Use EXP for powers of ten. Write units beside the result, not in the calculator.

title: Circuits
text:

Use these notes with the matching teaching slides and question sheet.

Parallel circuits: common voltage, branch currents, equivalent resistance, and power.
Series circuits: one current path, voltage drops, resistance, and power.
Series-parallel circuits: identify groups, reduce, solve, expand, and check.
Kirchhoff’s laws: write current and voltage equations for networks that do not reduce directly.
Linear algebra for circuits: solve several node or loop equations together.

Linear Algebra for Circuits
text:
Solve and check
Use substitution or elimination for a small system. Use a simultaneous-equation or matrix solver for a larger system. Keep the variable order and units consistent, then substitute the answer into the original equations or calculate the residual:
\[
\mathbf{r}=A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}
\tag{4}\]
\[
\mathbf{r}\approx\mathbf{0}
\tag{5}\]
A large residual can flag a wrong sign, wrong measurement, or wiring fault.

Worked solutions
On the course calculator, the Casio fx-991ES PLUS C, press MODE, then 5 for EQN. Press 1 for two unknowns or 2 for three unknowns. NoteQuestion 2: Solve a two-by-two system





Enter the rows \((10,-4,6)\) and \((-4,12,3)\).
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
10 & -4 \\

=

Final answers: \(I_1=0.808\,\mathrm{mA}\) and \(I_2=0.519\,\mathrm{mA}\).

NoteQuestion 4: Solve a three-by-three system

title: Series Circuits
text:
Series and parallel
A series circuit has one path, so the current is the same everywhere. A parallel circuit has branches that share the same two nodes, so each branch has the same voltage.



Figure 1. Series-circuit reference schematic. The same current passes through every component. #


Opening any component stops current everywhere.
crumbs: 2. Package 2: Parallel Review and Series Circuits

title: Series Circuits
text:
General rules
\[
I_k = I_T
\tag{1}\]
\[
R_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} R_k
\tag{2}\]
\[
V_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} V_k
\tag{3}\]
\[
P_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} P_k = V_T I_T
\tag{4}\]
\[
I_T = \frac{V_T}{R_T}
\tag{5}\]
\[
V_k = I_T R_k
\tag{6}\]
Here, \(k\) means any component in the path. Keep full calculator precision until the final answer.
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n} V_k \overset{?}{=} V_T
\tag{7}\]
Use Equation Equation 7 to check the voltage drops. Also check power ratings.

title: Series Circuits
text:
Worked solutions
Questions 2 and 4 are provided as student models. Complete the other questions independently using the same GUESS structure.






NoteQuestion 2: Complete series analysis





Given: \(V_T=15.0\,\mathrm{V}\), \(R_1=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_2=2.2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_3=3.3\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\).
\[
R_T=R_1+R_2+R_3=6.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
\tag{8}\]
\[
I_T=\frac{V_T}{R_T}=\frac{15.0\,\mathrm{V}}{6.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}=2.307692\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}
\tag{9}\]
Using \(V_k=I_TR_k\) gives \(V_1=2.307692\ldots\,\mathrm{V}\), \(V_2=5.076923\ldots\,\mathrm{V}\), and \(V_3=7.615385\ldots\,\mathrm{V}\).
Final answers: \(R_T=6.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(I_T=2.3\,\mathrm{mA}\), \(V_1=2.3\,\mathrm{V}\), \(V_2=5.1\,\mathrm{V}\), \(V_3=7.6\,\mathrm{V}\), and \(P_T=35\,\mathrm{mW}\).
Check: Use the unrounded values: \(V_1+V_2+V_3=15.0\,\mathrm{V}\).









NoteQuestion 4: Choose a dropping resistor





Given: a \(6.0\,\mathrm{V}\), \(80\,\mathrm{mA}\) lamp on a \(9.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source.
\[
V_R=V_T-V_L=9.0\,\mathrm{V}-6.0\,\mathrm{V}=3.0\,\mathrm{V}
\tag{10}\]
\[
R=\frac{V_R}{I}=\frac{3.0\,\mathrm{V}}{80\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}}=37.5\,\Omega
\tag{11}\]
\[
P_R=V_RI=(3.0\,\mathrm{V})(80\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A})=0.240\,\mathrm{W}
\tag{12}\]
Final answer: the calculated value is \(37.5\,\Omega\). Choose the next common 5% value, \(39\,\Omega\), rated for at least \(0.5\,\mathrm{W}\).
Key note: A \(0.25\,\mathrm{W}\) resistor is too close to the calculated \(0.240\,\mathrm{W}\) load.

title: Monitors, Signals, Ports, and Cables
section: Analog and digital in three steps
text:
Analog and digital in three steps




A grey continuous analog waveform with red digital samples over it.





1Analog waveform changes continuously


2Measure it at set intervals


3Represent samples as digital values


Figure 1. Grey is the continuous source signal. Red points are discrete, quantized digital samples. Public-domain image by Rbj and wdwd. Open image source.
VGA is analog. Noise can appear as blur, colour shifts, or ghosting.
HDMI, DisplayPort, Mini DisplayPort, USB-C video, and DVI-D are digital. A weak digital link may show sparkles, dropouts, or no picture. DVI-A is analog. DVI-I can carry both.

title: Monitors, Signals, Ports, and Cables
section: Match the port to the cable
text:
Match the port to the cable
Each pair shows a cable plug and the matching computer or display port.


 

VGA
Analog video. Usually no audio. Tighten the two thumb screws gently.

Cable source · port source




 

DVI
DVI-D is digital. DVI-A is analog. DVI-I supports both. Check the pin pattern before connecting.

Cable source · port source




 

HDMI
Digital video and audio. Common on monitors, televisions, laptops, and game consoles.

Cable source · port source




 

DisplayPort
Digital video and audio. The full-size connector has one clipped corner.

Cable source · port source




 

Mini DisplayPort
The same DisplayPort signal in a smaller connector. Thunderbolt 1 and 2 use the same shape, so check the symbol.

Cable source · port source




 

FireWire / IEEE 1394
A legacy digital peripheral connection for cameras, audio interfaces, and external drives. It is not a normal monitor connection.

Cable source · port source




 

USB-C video
The shape alone does not promise video. The computer port, cable, adapter or dock, and monitor must support the same video path.

Strip about 25 to 40 mm. Cut lightly. Do not nick the eight insulated conductors.



2

Inspect every conductor
If copper is exposed or insulation is cut, remove the damaged section and start again.



3

Untangle and flatten
Separate the four pairs. Untwist only the length needed to reach the plug.



4

Arrange T568B
Place all eight conductors in the colour order shown above.



5

Trim to an even 13 mm
Pinch the order between your fingers. Cut the ends straight and even.



6

Insert and verify
Clip down, gold pins up, white-orange on the left. Every wire reaches the front. About 6 mm of jacket enters the plug.



7

Crimp
Insert the plug fully into the correct crimper slot. Squeeze completely using the demonstrated tool procedure.



8

Inspect the termination
All contacts sit evenly. The strain relief grips the jacket. Gently tug the cable.



9

Finish the other end and test
Use T568B again. A good tester shows pins 1 through 8 in the same order at both ends.








Outer jacket being removed from an Ethernet cable.



Steps 1 and 2
Remove only the jacket, then inspect the inner insulation.
Figure 3. Open source and licence.






Twisted pairs separated for Ethernet termination.



Step 3
Separate the pairs and keep the untwisted length short.
Figure 4. Open source and licence.






Ethernet conductors aligned before entering the modular plug.



Steps 4 to 6
Order, flatten, trim, insert, and check through the clear plug.
Figure 5. Open source and licence.






A photo sequence showing an 8P8C plug being inserted and crimped.



Steps 7 and 8
Crimp fully. Check contact height and strain relief before testing.
Figure 6. Public-domain visual sequence. Open source.






Network cable tester used for modular Ethernet cables.



Step 9
Test for correct order, opens, shorts, reversals, crossed pairs, and split pairs.
Figure 7. Open source and licence.

title: How Wi-Fi and Ethernet Connect
text:
Wi-Fi is not the Internet. Ethernet is not the Internet. Both are ways to join a local network.
Figure 1. One local network can use Wi-Fi and Ethernet at the same time. Open image source and licence.

title: How Wi-Fi and Ethernet Connect
text:
Switch or router?





Five-port Ethernet switch.



Switch: same local network
Learns which device is on each port and forwards Ethernet frames using MAC addresses. It gives the class more Ethernet ports. It does not normally create the Internet connection.
Figure 2. Classroom-style switch. Open source and licence.



Router: between networks
Forwards IP packets between different networks. The school router or gateway connects the classroom network toward the Internet.
A home Wi-Fi router combines several jobs in one box: router, switch, Wi-Fi access point, DHCP, NAT, and firewall.

title: How Wi-Fi and Ethernet Connect
text:
Classroom path
COMPUTER → ETHERNET CABLE → CLASS SWITCH → SCHOOL ROUTER/GATEWAY → INTERNET SERVICE

Access point: provides the Wi-Fi radio link.
DHCP: gives a device local network settings.
DNS: translates a name such as example.org into an IP address.
Modem or ONT: connects a customer network to cable, DSL, fibre, or another provider link.

Quick check: if Wi-Fi connects but websites do not load, test local IP settings, gateway reachability, DNS, and Internet service separately.

title: Choosing a Linux Distribution
text:
A Linux distribution, or distro, is a complete operating system built around Linux. Distros are a little like different flavours: they share many ingredients, but each has its own installer, desktop, software choices, update system, and community. No flavour is best for everyone, although people often have strong preferences. Some distributions are also based on other distributions.
For example:
Debian
└── Ubuntu
    ├── Ubuntu Desktop
    ├── Xubuntu
    ├── Lubuntu
    └── Linux Mint
        ├── Cinnamon edition
        ├── MATE edition
        └── Xfce edition
Debian is a long-running, community-built distribution known for stability. Ubuntu is based on Debian and aims to make Linux practical for a wide range of users. The African word ubuntu is often translated as “I am because we are.” Xubuntu and Lubuntu are Ubuntu flavours. Linux Mint is Ubuntu-based and provides Cinnamon, MATE, and Xfce editions.
A distribution packages the operating system, installer, software sources, update policy, and support community. A desktop environment supplies the graphical workspace, menus, panels, and common tools. Linux Mint is a distribution; Xfce is one desktop environment it can use.

title: Choosing a Linux Distribution
text:
Our choice: Linux Mint Xfce
We will use Linux Mint 22.3 “Zena” Xfce Edition because it works well and is easy for students to begin using. Xfce is the desktop interface. Its layout feels a little like older versions of Windows, and it runs quickly on our older computers with less than 8 GB of RAM. It starts simple, but we can improve and personalize the way it looks later.
Lubuntu is another good lightweight flavour to explore. If you want to compare many possibilities, try the questions at Distrochooser.

title: Choosing a Linux Distribution
section: Release styles: a stable base or the newest software
text:
Release styles: a stable base or the newest software
Ubuntu publishes a new version every six months, usually in April and October. Its version number shows the year and month: 24.04 means April 2024. Releases also have names, such as Ubuntu 24.04 “Noble Numbat.”
Every two years, the April release is an LTS, or Long Term Support, release. LTS versions receive updates for much longer than the releases between them, making them a dependable base for a classroom or everyday computer. Linux Mint 22.3 “Zena” uses the Ubuntu 24.04 LTS package base and is supported until April 2029. We can keep an LTS-based system for work and experiment with a faster-moving distribution on another computer, in a virtual machine, or later as part of a dual-boot setup.
Arch uses a rolling-release model instead of publishing separate LTS versions on a fixed timetable. You install it once and update it continuously, so new software arrives quickly. This gives you current software and a great deal of control, but it also asks you to read update notices, make decisions, and troubleshoot more often.
Arch Linux is the most difficult option discussed here. It expects you to assemble and configure much more of the system yourself. That makes it a poor first classroom installation, but a valuable future challenge if you want to become a system administrator and understand or control every part of a Linux system.
In my classes, students who chose Arch and persisted through its difficulties have often gone on to considerable success in computer engineering, including major scholarship and job opportunities. Arch itself is not a shortcut to those outcomes. The persistence, research, troubleshooting, and systems thinking required to make it work are excellent preparation.
For this lab, our choice is Linux Mint Xfce. In a future lab, we will choose another operating system and install it alongside Windows to create a dual-boot computer.

title: Files, Folders, Terminal, and Permissions
text:
Safe practice workspace
Sign in to your own account and create one practice directory:
mkdir -p ~/linux-labs/files-practice
cd ~/linux-labs/files-practice
pwd
Use pwd before every group of commands. Practise with ls, mkdir, touch, cp, mv, cat, less, and rm. Use rm only on teacher-approved practice files. Do not use sudo, wildcards with rm, or commands copied from an unknown site.
Compare the same folder in Thunar File Manager. Turn on hidden files and find .bash_history. Do not edit or submit private information.

title: Files, Folders, Terminal, and Permissions
text:
Permissions
Create a file, then inspect it:
touch team-notes.txt
ls -l team-notes.txt
Learn what the read, write, and execute positions mean for the owner, group, and others. Use chmod only on the practice file and verify the result with ls -l.

title: Files, Folders, Terminal, and Permissions
text:
Evidence
This follow-up lesson is separate from Terminal Quest. If your teacher assigns evidence for it, provide a short command transcript, a screenshot showing the same folder in the terminal and GUI, and an explanation of why checking pwd reduces mistakes. Follow the submission location and file count provided in Google Classroom. Do not add this evidence to Terminal Quest unless your teacher explicitly asks.

title: Files, Folders, Terminal, and Permissions
section: Everyday Python project: Downloads Folder Helper
text:
Everyday Python project: Downloads Folder Helper
Write a Python program using pathlib that reads a teacher-approved practice folder and reports how many files have each extension. Add a dry-run mode that prints proposed moves without changing any files. Only after reviewing the output should the program organize copies inside the practice folder.
Never test a new file-management program on your real Downloads folder, shared folders, or another student’s files. A safe automation shows what it plans to do and stays inside a clearly bounded location.

Continue Bashcrawl or begin OverTheWire Bandit only with a teacher-approved account.

title: Know Your Linux Computer
text:
Start with the GUI
Open System Info from the Linux Mint menu. Record the operating system, Xfce version, processor, installed memory, graphics device, and storage information. Then open Task Manager and observe CPU and memory use while no large application is open.
Open a browser and Software Manager. Watch what changes. A computer can have 8 GB of RAM installed without having all 8 GB available because Linux and open applications are using some of it.

title: Know Your Linux Computer
text:
Confirm it in the terminal
Run one command at a time. Read the output before continuing.






NoteBegin with Terminal Quest



If you have not completed the cross-platform terminal basics, make a copy of Terminal Quest: WSL and Mac Basics. It explains how to open WSL, Linux Terminal, or macOS Terminal, run beginner commands, inspect processes, and paste a reviewed command history into one Google Doc.


lscpu
free -h
lsblk
df -h
lspci
ip address
Example free -h output:
               total        used        free      available
Mem:           7.7Gi       2.1Gi       3.8Gi          5.3Gi
Swap:          2.0Gi          0B       2.0Gi
Example lsblk output:
NAME   SIZE TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
sda  238.5G disk
├─sda1  512M part /boot/efi
└─sda2  238G part /
Your device names and values will differ. Focus on what each column means rather than copying the example.
Use lscpu for processor information, free -h for memory, lsblk for storage devices, df -h for used and available space, lspci for internal hardware, and ip address for network interfaces.
Install htop from Software Manager if it is not already available, then run:
htop
Observe the processor meters, memory meter, process list, and load average. Press q to quit. Do not end a process unless your teacher approves it.

title: Know Your Linux Computer
section: Everyday Python project: My Computer Report
text:
Everyday Python project: My Computer Report
Create a small Python program named computer_report.py. It should print the operating system, computer name, processor description, Python version, and total, used, and free space in your home drive. Begin with Python’s built-in platform and shutil modules so the program also works in WSL and on a Mac.
Run it from the terminal and compare its answers with System Info and the Linux commands above. Add the program to your Git repository later. Your report must not include passwords, serial numbers, public IP addresses, access tokens, or private information about another student.

title: From Linux Computer to Raspberry Pi
text:
Readiness sequence
Before receiving a Raspberry Pi, complete these checkpoints:

Use voltage, current, and power relationships to check the required supply and connected loads.
Explain connector polarity and why voltage compatibility is not enough without adequate current capacity.
Identify the intended operating system image, storage device, hostname, accounts, and network method.
Plan how the image and project files will be backed up and recovered.
Decide which work happens locally and which work happens through SSH.
Prepare a small Git repository with a README, Python test program, data folder, and Quarto documentation page.
Draw the complete system boundary: supply, Pi, storage, network, sensors, outputs, and user.

The first Raspberry Pi lab should reuse familiar skills: boot Linux, identify hardware, update safely, clone a repository, run Python, record data, connect with SSH, use tmux, and publish results. Only then should students add sensors and control outputs.

title: Analyze Data and Fit a Curve with Python
text:
Progression

Load the CSV produced in the previous lesson.
Check row count, column names, units, missing values, and impossible values.
Plot the raw points before fitting anything.
Begin with a linear model using a teacher dataset such as voltage versus current.
Plot the fitted line on the same axes.
Calculate residuals: measured value minus predicted value.
Explain the slope, intercept, fit quality, and whether the model is physically reasonable.
Publish the graph and interpretation on the Quarto site, then commit and push the update.

Later datasets may use polynomial or nonlinear models, but the model must come from the system and evidence, not from trying random equations.

title: Analyze Data and Fit a Curve with Python
text:
Evidence
Submit the code, labelled graph, model equation, residual plot or table, and a paragraph connecting the result to the original measurement problem.

title: Analyze Data and Fit a Curve with Python
text:
Extend your learning

Use the Matplotlib quick-start guide.
Compare a fit with and without one suspicious measurement, then justify whether that point should remain.
Add uncertainty or repeated trials when the measurement process supports them.

title: Analyze Data and Fit a Curve with Python
text:
Review and reflect
What does the slope represent in your system? What can a residual plot reveal that a fitted line alone may hide?

title: Build a Website with Quarto
text:
Build in small steps

Confirm that Git and Quarto are installed with git --version and quarto --version.
Use a teacher template or create a basic Quarto website inside your Git repository.
Add a home page, an About me as a technologist page, and a Linux learning log page. Do not publish private information.
Preview locally with quarto preview.
Fix warnings and broken links.
Render the complete site with quarto render.
Open the generated site locally and test every navigation link.
Review git status, then commit only the intended source and configuration files.

Your first site should be simple. Clear headings, useful alt text, readable colour contrast, and working links matter more than effects.
